eventCatalog.name: Snow: the clock starts
eventCatalog.text: Snow stopped falling. The law gives you 4 hours in the daytime, or until 11 AM after an overnight fall, to open a 4-foot path along your whole frontage. Sanitation agents are out writing tickets.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NOAA daily snowfall at Central Park (GHCN-Daily station USW00094728, element SNOW >= 0.1 in) and the hour the snow ended; DSNY Snow Alert notices
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 11 days a season with measurable snow (climate table in the engine). Normal season snowfall is 29.8 inches; the last four seasons brought 2.3, 7.5, 12.9 and, by press count, 43.4 inches. Enforcement in January-March 2026: 9,456 summonses for snow and ice on sidewalks (5,852 in January, 3,481 in February) and 54,089 complaints to 311.
eventCatalog.note: Deadlines opened in the NYC311 article; summons and complaint counts are my queries of NYC Open Data (OATH hearings, charge AS21; 311 requests, complaint type 'Snow or Ice', January 20-March 15, 2026). Of January-February summonses that reached a hearing date, 4,379 defaulted. The $30 is one snowfall of the staff option: 1.5 hours at $17.00 plus ice melt. The 0.85 day multiplier is the snow value already in ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json; this event adds the duty and the ticket, not a second drop.

eventCatalog.name: Black ice at the door
eventCatalog.text: Yesterday's slush froze overnight. If your stretch of sidewalk is the icy one, people cross the street instead of walking past your window, and the first fall is yours to answer for.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Central Park snow depth above zero (GHCN SNWD) with a daily low at or below 32°F on the days after a snowfall; NWS Special Weather Statement for black ice
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows most snowfalls: January's normal low at Central Park is 27.8°F and February's 29.6°F, so slush refreezes overnight for one to three nights. In January-February 2026 the cold after the January 25 storm kept ice on sidewalks for more than a week.
eventCatalog.note: The user's own example. No study measures how many passers-by avoid an icy storefront; 0.85 on icy days for a shop that did not clear is my estimate, set equal to the snow-day drop. Month value: 3 icy days x 15% / 30 = 1.5%, rounded to 0.98. A shop that cleared its walk gets no penalty.

eventCatalog.name: Letter from a lawyer: someone fell on your ice
eventCatalog.text: A pedestrian slipped in front of your shop on a day you did not clear the snow. Their lawyer has written to the building owner, and your lease says you pay the owner back.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Not a public signal: the claim follows from the player's own record. It is created when a snowfall deadline passed with snow_ice_plan = none (or the shortcut on) and arrives two to four months later
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The Hartford, 2025: slips, falls and customer injuries are 20% of small-business liability claims, twice the 2015 share; the average claim is $45,000 and the average liability claim $97,200.
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic by rule 4: the claim exists only if the walk was left uncleared, and only once per winter. $2,500 = deductible and legal time (planning value); the 25% premium increase for a year after a paid claim is my estimate, no public rate table was found. A court can only hold the tenant itself liable if the lease or its own shoveling made things worse (Cruz v Heights Broadway, First Department 2023); the usual route is the lease's indemnity clause.

eventCatalog.name: Slush on the floor
eventCatalog.text: Every customer walks in with snow on their boots. By ten o'clock the tile by the door is a skating rink, and the line stands right on it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Any day with rain or snow in the forecast (NWS point forecast for New York, NY); days with precipitation of 0.01 in or more at Central Park
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Central Park has about 10 to 11 days with precipitation in every month of the year (1991-2020 normals).
eventCatalog.note: The quality effect is a design value. The money risk sits in the wet_floor_fall_claim record: with 'nothing' chosen through a whole winter the engine raises one claim, as with the sidewalk.

eventCatalog.name: Blizzard warning: the city tells people to stay home
eventCatalog.text: A foot or more of snow is forecast. Schools go remote, above-ground trains may stop, and the mayor asks everyone to stay off the roads. Half your staff cannot get in and the street is empty.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS New York (OKX) Winter Storm Warning or Blizzard Warning for New York (Manhattan) County; NYC Emergency Management travel advisory; MTA service alerts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Two in the 2025-26 winter by press reports: January 25, 2026 (11.4 inches in Central Park) and a February 2026 blizzard (19.7 inches). Many winters have none: the National Weather Service table gives 2.3 inches for the whole 2022-23 season, 7.5 for 2023-24 and 12.9 for 2024-25, against a normal of 29.8.
eventCatalog.note: The deck's 'storm' day is 0.7; a warned blizzard is worse. 0.4 on the storm day and the day after is my estimate from Foursquare's 'up to 40% drop in major weather events' (already cited in nyc-climate.json) and Placer.ai's 20-30% storm-week losses in the hardest-hit states. Month value: 2 days x 60% / 30 = 4%. Delivery falls too: the city has suspended e-bike delivery during the worst hours of past storms. Season totals for 2022-25 were opened in the NWS seasonal snowfall table.

eventCatalog.name: Ice melt sold out
eventCatalog.text: A storm is two days away and every hardware store within a mile is out of rock salt. Shops that bought their bags in November are fine. The rest are shoveling twice and hoping.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Local hardware store and distributor stock reports before a forecast storm; New York State road-salt contract prices (OGS award: $52.87-$99.90 a ton for 2025-26, average $72.32)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: January and February 2026: stores in the Hudson Valley and Yonkers sold out before the storms and blamed their distributors (News 12); shortages were reported across the Northeast and Midwest.
eventCatalog.note: The contractor option of snow_ice_plan is immune (the crew brings its own salt). For the staff option the engine adds a second shoveling pass and a marked-up bag: $60 is a planning value. No retail price per 50 lb bag in New York in 2026 was found.

eventCatalog.name: A sidewalk shed goes up over your door
eventCatalog.text: The building has to inspect its facade. A green plywood tunnel now covers your sign and your window. Nobody can tell you when it comes down: the average one in the city has been up for a year and a half.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Open Data 'DOB NOW: Build - Approved Permits' (data set rbx6-tga4), work type 'Sidewalk Shed', by building identification number; the building's facade inspection filing window (Local Law 11): every building over six stories files every five years
eventCatalog.realFrequency: My count from NYC Open Data (DOB NOW approved permits, work type Sidewalk Shed, permits not yet expired on November 14, 2026): 6,889 buildings, of them 3,117 in Manhattan, 1,736 in Brooklyn, 1,136 in the Bronx, 840 in Queens and 60 on Staten Island. The Mayor's Office counted 7,427 permitted sheds on August 17, 2026. The average shed permit was 557 days old in March 2026 (West Side Rag, from the same data).
eventCatalog.note: Mayor's Office with Mastercard, August 2024: Manhattan businesses under a shed lost $3,900-$9,500 a month in card spending, and restaurants and bars saw weekly transactions fall 3.5-9.7% in the six months after the shed went up; longer sheds hurt most. 0.93 = midpoint. Duration 18 months = 557 days. Not random in the game: the place carries the building's height and filing year, so the player can see it coming before signing the lease.

eventCatalog.name: The shed is up and nobody is working
eventCatalog.text: Three months in, there has not been a single worker on the scaffold. Under the 2025 law the owner now pays the city for every idle month, and that is your one lever to get the work moving.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Buildings Department permit status for the address: shed permit active with no open work permit; 311 complaints about the shed
eventCatalog.realFrequency: More than 300 sheds had been standing over five years in April 2025.
eventCatalog.note: Local Law 48 of 2025 as quoted by web search: shed permits last 90 days instead of a year and cannot be renewed until penalties are paid; where no work is in progress the owner pays $10 per linear foot of shed per month for a shed under three years old and $100 at three to four years, capped at $6,000 a month. Local Law 51: $5,000-$20,000 if permitted facade repair is not finished within two years. The effect is the same shed penalty continued; the lever option press_the_owner is the response.

eventCatalog.name: The shed comes down
eventCatalog.text: The scaffolding is gone. Daylight hits your window for the first time in a year, and people who walked past every day ask if you are new.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Buildings Department: shed permit expired or signed off for the address; citywide count of permitted sheds
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 1,200 fewer sheds between January 1 and October 19, 2026, a 15% decline (Mayor's Office).
eventCatalog.note: The penalty ends; the short +3% is my estimate for the reopening effect (a storefront that looks new), no measurement was found.

eventCatalog.name: No trains at your station on weekends
eventCatalog.text: The MTA is replacing signals. For the next months there is no service at your stop on most weekends, only shuttle buses that nobody likes. Saturday and Sunday are your best days.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA planned service changes (mta.info 'Planned Work' and the GTFS-realtime alerts feed) for the nearest station; MTA 'Subway Hourly Ridership' open data on data.ny.gov shows the drop
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Greenpoint, July 2025-July 2026: the G train was out on about 40% of weekends since signal work began in 2024. The MTA cancelled the shutdowns planned for December 2026 after business owners protested.
eventCatalog.note: Shop Small Greenpoint survey of 36 businesses (an interested party): 91% saw sales fall on shutdown weekends, by 20-24% on average; 39% cut shifts. One coffee shop owner: 'A day like today we'd see 200 people, and now we are down to half of that.' Day value 0.78 = 22% drop. Month value: two shutdown weekends (4 days) x 22% / 30 = 3%. Staff who commute on the same line arrive late or not at all.

eventCatalog.name: Your subway station closes for renovation
eventCatalog.text: The station at your corner shuts completely for a rebuild. The stream of commuters that passed your door twice a day now walks to the next stop, in the other direction.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA capital program station projects and station closure notices; MTA station entries (turnstile data) for the complex
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Astoria, October 2017-June 2018: the 30th Avenue and 36th Avenue stations were closed for eight months; the next pair on the line followed.
eventCatalog.note: Owners near the closed Astoria stations told reporters they had lost 25-30% (a grocery) and 30-40% (a gastropub); some shops closed for good. 0.72 = middle of those anecdotes for a shop that lives on station traffic; a shop on a residential side street would lose far less. The engine should scale the loss by the share of the place's footfall that comes from the station (data/open/fit.json has it).

eventCatalog.name: The street is dug up for a new water main
eventCatalog.text: Fences, steel plates and a trench run the length of your block. The crew will be here for a year or more. The sidewalk is open, but nobody wants to walk through a construction site for coffee.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC DOT 'Street Construction Permits' open data for the block; Department of Design and Construction project pages and community construction liaison notices
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Routine: water mains from the early 1900s are being replaced block by block. A Myrtle Avenue project in Brooklyn replaced pipes laid in 1908.
eventCatalog.note: The only New York figure found for a water main job: a West 10th Street shoe repair shop's receipts fell 10-15%. 0.87 = midpoint. The City's Small Business Services FAQ (2022) says it has no program or grant to reimburse lost revenue from construction; the one exception on record, after the Fulton Street water main, paid $2.50 per square foot per month up to $25,000 in 2007-2008. Dust and mud also mean more sweeping, hence the sidewalk lever.

eventCatalog.name: Water off on your block, weekdays 8 to 3
eventCatalog.text: The city is replacing a main and will shut the water two to four days a week for the next five weeks, right through your morning rush. No water means no espresso, no hand washing and no legal way to stay open.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Department of Environmental Protection and Department of Design and Construction shutoff notices posted on the block and sent to the community board
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Garment District, Manhattan: an emergency main replacement brought shutoffs two to four days a week from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. for up to five weeks.
eventCatalog.note: Three shutoff days a week x 7 of 12 opening hours, weighted to the morning when about two thirds of coffee is sold: roughly 12 lost days of morning trade in a month = -20% (my arithmetic). The Health Code requires running hot and cold water to operate; serving through a shutoff is a closure-level violation that D08 should carry.

eventCatalog.name: Water main breaks on your block
eventCatalog.text: An old cast-iron main gave way in the cold. The street is a river, the basement is taking water, and the block will have no water until the crew finishes the repair.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DEP water main break count (Mayor's Management Report); 311 water main complaints; a run of freeze-thaw days at Central Park
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the Comptroller's audit of the leak detection program: the city repaired 1,314 water main breaks from fiscal 2023 through fiscal 2025, and breaks 'rose by 54% compared to FY24' in fiscal 2025; only 42 of the 1,314 were found by the program's own surveys. Not opened: 359 breaks in fiscal 2024 against a five-year average of 427, and the winter freeze-thaw pattern (Mayor's Management Report).
eventCatalog.note: Rule 4: the engine does not roll for a break. The world schedules a fixed number of breaks per winter from the real count and assigns them to blocks with the oldest mains; the block is told one game day ahead (the street is already leaking). One to two days without water = -5% of a month. $1,500 = spoiled stock and cleanup in an unprotected basement (planning value). Damage from a city main can be claimed from the Comptroller, but a notice of claim must be filed within 90 days.

eventCatalog.name: Milling and paving
eventCatalog.text: No parking on the block from 7 AM. The machines strip the asphalt today and lay new tomorrow. Your delivery cannot stop, and the dust comes in every time the door opens.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC DOT weekly resurfacing schedule by borough; temporary no-parking signs posted 72 hours ahead
eventCatalog.realFrequency: DOT repaves in the warm months; each block comes up once in roughly a decade.
eventCatalog.note: No measurement found; 10% on two days is my estimate, far below the long-dig figure. The real cost is the missed delivery: order a day early. The once-a-decade frequency is from memory.

eventCatalog.name: Street fair on your avenue
eventCatalog.text: Ten blocks of sock stalls, grilled corn and lemonade stand between the crowd and your door. Thousands walk past. Most of them buy their coffee from the cart parked in front of your window.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Street Activity Permit Office calendar ('NYC Permitted Event Information' open data), event type Street Festival
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The city stopped issuing permits for new street fairs in October 2024 because of police overtime costs; existing fairs continue, one or two Sundays a year on a given avenue.
eventCatalog.note: Correction to the event deck, where a street fair is a flat +20% of foot traffic. Store owners have complained for years that fairs put vendors between the crowd and their doors; some shop owners do well by setting up a table of their own. No measured figure exists. My model: 60% more people on the street, but a shop that does nothing converts 30% fewer of them (stalls block the storefront and sell drinks); with the window menu the shop keeps its conversion and gains. Deliveries cannot reach the block.

eventCatalog.name: A film crew takes the block
eventCatalog.text: Orange cones went up last night: 'No parking, film shoot.' Trucks line both curbs for three days, cables cross the sidewalk, and a production assistant asks your customers to wait while they roll.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Mayor's Office of Media and Entertainment 'Film Permits' open data (street segments and dates); no-parking notices posted on the block
eventCatalog.realFrequency: My count from NYC Open Data 'Film Permits': 5,491 permits starting in 2025 (Manhattan 2,860, Brooklyn 1,787, Queens 657, the Bronx 108, Staten Island 79) and 6,278 in 2024; 3,497 so far in 2026. Some blocks in SoHo, the Village and Brooklyn Heights are permitted many times a year; most blocks never.
eventCatalog.note: There is no city compensation: owners on Crosby Street said frequent shoots cost them walk-in sales and that the film office never answered. The film office limits parking taken and calls it 'an inconvenience'. A production that wants your storefront in the shot pays a negotiated location fee, and a crew of 50-100 buys coffee: +5% for a shop that staffs up is my estimate. 0.9 is an estimate, not measured.

eventCatalog.name: Your street goes car-free on weekends
eventCatalog.text: A neighborhood group won an Open Streets permit. From April to October the block is closed to cars on weekends: strollers, chalk, a band on the corner, and room for tables.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC DOT Open Streets locations and hours (open data and nyc.gov/openstreets); the annual application round that closes in winter
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the Comptroller's 'Streets for People': 'At its peak in 2021, there were 326 open streets throughout New York City. Just two years later, the number of open streets had dropped by 40% to 202 sites.' DOT announced more than 150 at the start of the 2026 season (press release, not opened).
eventCatalog.note: DOT's 'Streets for Recovery' (2022, sales-tax data): sales on five Open Streets corridors were 19% above the pre-pandemic baseline while nearby control corridors were 29% below; City Planning (2024) found storefront vacancy 12% lower than the city average. Those are corridor totals driven by restaurants with new outdoor tables and by pandemic conditions; +5% of foot traffic for a counter-service cafe over the whole month is my conservative reading. Deliveries must come before the closure hours. A volunteer group runs it and can lose its funding: the event can end between seasons. Second pass: the program counts were opened at the Comptroller; the sales figures (+19% against -29%) are still from the DOT release as quoted by search.

eventCatalog.name: Congestion Relief Zone: more people on foot
eventCatalog.text: Fewer cars cross 60th Street, and more people arrive by train and walk. Inside the zone the sidewalks are fuller than last year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA 'Congestion Relief Zone Vehicle Entries' open data (data.ny.gov); pedestrian counts published by the state and by the Economic Development Corporation

effects.onlyIf: place is in Manhattan south of 60th Street

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the Governor's first-anniversary release (January 5, 2026): 27 million fewer vehicles entered the zone, an 11% reduction; 'Foot traffic increased by 3.4 percent in the zone, compared to a boroughwide increase of 1.4 percent'; one percentage point fewer vacant storefronts in the zone; sales tax receipts in the city up 6.3% in 2025 through November.
eventCatalog.note: 1.02 = the difference between the zone and the rest of the borough (3.4% - 1.4%). The figures come from the program's sponsor. Applies only to places inside the zone.

eventCatalog.name: Suppliers add a congestion surcharge
eventCatalog.text: Your dairy and paper-goods distributors now add a line to every invoice for deliveries below 60th Street. Each truck pays the toll every time it enters the zone.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA Congestion Relief Zone toll schedule; supplier invoices

effects.onlyIf: place is in Manhattan south of 60th Street

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Permanent. Rates are fixed through 2027; in 2028 the car toll rises to $12 and the large-truck toll to $28.80, and in 2031 to $15 and $36.
eventCatalog.note: Peak tolls with E-ZPass: cars $9 once a day, small trucks $14.40 and large trucks $21.60 on every entry; overnight $2.25, $3.60 and $5.40. Arithmetic: a truck that makes 15 drops in the zone on one entry adds about $1 to $1.50 a drop; five deliveries a week = about $25 a month on roughly $13,000 of goods, so the honest effect is 0.2%. Distributors charge more than cost: a flat $5-$10 per delivery is reported but unsourced; that would be $100-$200 a month, about 1% of cost of goods. The deck uses +2%; I suggest +1%. Opened the Governor's release: truck speeds in the zone were up 5.6% on 2024, so a delivery route takes less time than before the toll.

eventCatalog.name: A protected bike lane replaces the parking
eventCatalog.text: The city is redesigning your avenue: a bike lane at the curb, parking moved out, loading zones on the corners. Half the merchants on the block signed a petition against it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC DOT street improvement project list and community board presentations for the corridor
eventCatalog.realFrequency: DOT builds protected bike lanes on dozens of miles of streets a year.
eventCatalog.note: DOT, 'The Economic Benefits of Sustainable Streets' (2013, sales-tax data): on Ninth Avenue between 23rd and 31st Streets, sales at local businesses rose up to 49% in the three years after the protected bike lane, against 3% across Manhattan. DOT itself says this does not prove the lane caused it. +3% is my cautious value; the non-obvious part is the sign: merchants expect a loss and the data shows none. One to two months of construction first (use street_resurfacing for those).

eventCatalog.name: A coffee cart parks at your corner
eventCatalog.text: A cart selling $2 coffee and $1.50 bagels now sets up at the subway stairs every morning at six. It pays no rent, and it catches the commuters before they reach your door.
eventCatalog.realSignal: New mobile food vending permits issued under Local Laws 54 and 59 of 2026 (Health Department permit data); 311 vending complaints for the block
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened NYC311 'Food Cart Vendor Permit': Local Law 18 of 2021 raised the cap by 445 supervisory licenses a year in fiscal 2023-2026; Local Laws 54 and 59 of 2026 raise it by 2,200 a year in fiscal 2027-2031 (500 citywide, 1,500 outside Manhattan, 200 for disabled people and veterans): 11,000 more carts in five years.
eventCatalog.note: No study of what a cart costs a neighboring cafe was found: -4% is my estimate (the cart takes the cheapest drip-coffee orders in the morning rush, not the latte or the seat). Placement rules, read from the charges in the OATH hearings data set for 2026: a cart may not vend on a sidewalk less than 12 feet wide or away from the curb (466 summonses), touch or lean against a building (349), or stand in a bus stop or next to a hospital (599). A cart that breaks one of these can be reported to 311; one that follows them is legal competition. The legal answers are an earlier opening hour, a faster line and a product the cart does not have.

eventCatalog.name: Marathon Sunday on your avenue
eventCatalog.text: The race runs past your door. From early morning the avenue is fenced, nobody can cross, and deliveries cannot come. On your side of the barrier there are thousands of spectators with cold hands.
eventCatalog.realSignal: New York Road Runners course map and the city street-closure list for the first Sunday of November (November 1, 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year on the course: Fourth Avenue and Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn, First Avenue and Fifth Avenue in Manhattan, and shorter stretches in Queens and the Bronx.
eventCatalog.note: The deck has a citywide +10%; on the course itself the day is different. In 2026 the organizers changed the Bronx route for the first time in 15 years, and gave restoring access to local businesses as the main reason: a supermarket and a laundromat had been cut off inside the course. +50% of people at the door for a shop on the spectator side is my estimate; a shop whose regulars live across the avenue loses them for the day. Staff need a route to work that does not cross the course.

eventCatalog.name: Iced season starts
eventCatalog.text: The first run of 70-degree days. By Friday more than half of your orders are iced, the ice bin is empty by two o'clock, and you are out of cold cups.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Daily high at Central Park (NWS forecast and GHCN TMAX): the first week with highs of 65°F or more
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year: the normal high passes 62°F in April and 72°F in May.
eventCatalog.note: The share comes from extra.drinkMixByTemperature (April 38%, May 50% against March 24%; the London curve without my New York offset gives 23%, 35% and 9%). Square's own transaction data for a British heatwave weekend in May 2026 showed iced coffee purchases up 137% on the weekend before, and 47% of people it surveyed switch to iced when it is hot. The +1% on cost of goods is my estimate for the plastic cup, lid, straw and ice of an iced drink against a paper cup; D04 owns the exact figure. A shop that has not stocked cold cups or sized its ice machine loses the orders, not just the margin.

eventCatalog.name: Heat wave: everyone wants it iced
eventCatalog.text: Four days above 90. Nobody orders a hot latte. The line is as long as ever, but every drink needs ice, and your machine makes less of it the hotter the room gets.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS Heat Advisory or Extreme Heat Warning for New York City; NYC Emergency Management heat emergency declaration; Central Park daily highs of 90°F or more
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the NWS table of 90°F days at Central Park: on average 15 a year (3 in June, 7 in July, 4 in August, 1 in September); 24 in 2022, 12 in 2023, 21 in 2024, 14 in 2025. On July 2, 2026 Central Park reached 100°F for the first time since July 18, 2012, and a second heat wave followed in mid-July (press).
eventCatalog.note: Correction to the deck, which cuts foot traffic 5% in heat: Foursquare with AccuWeather found restaurants lose visits on unusually hot days while coffee shop brands gain slightly, so traffic is held at 1.0 and the mix moves (73% iced at 90°F and the 80% cap from 96°F by the formula). Utilities +20% on the hot days is my estimate for an air conditioner and three compressors running flat out; month value 4 days / 30 x 20% = 3%.

eventCatalog.name: The air conditioner dies on the hottest day
eventCatalog.text: It is 97 outside and 88 inside. The unit that nobody serviced in spring has iced over. Every repair company in the city is booked for three days, and customers walk in, feel the air and walk out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Not a public signal: follows from cooling_plan = unserviced during the first declared heat emergency of the summer
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: breakdowns cluster in the first heat wave, when every unit in the city starts at once.
eventCatalog.note: Rule 4: no dice. The failure happens only to a shop that chose unserviced, in the first heat emergency of its summer. $900 = emergency call and a part at peak-season rates (planning value; D03 owns repair prices). -30% on three days is my estimate; month value 3%.

eventCatalog.name: Con Edison cuts voltage in your neighborhood
eventCatalog.text: The grid is at its limit. Con Edison has reduced voltage by 8% in your network and asks everyone to turn things off. Your grinder sounds tired, the fridge compressors run hot, and a full outage is one cable away.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Con Edison voltage-reduction notices by network and its outage map; New York Independent System Operator peak-load forecast
eventCatalog.realFrequency: June 24, 2025: 8% cut for about 150,200 customers in parts of Brooklyn and Queens; more than 100,000 customers lost power during that heat wave. July 2026: 8% cuts in the Bronx and Westchester, and service shut off to about 9,800 customers in southwest Queens for repairs.
eventCatalog.note: Capacity -10% on the affected days is my estimate (slower heat recovery on the espresso machine, staff switching equipment off). If the cut becomes an outage of more than 12 hours caused by Con Edison's local equipment, a business may claim spoiled perishables up to $12,900 within 30 days (opened NYC311: 'up to a maximum of $12,900 for actual losses of perishable merchandise'; storm outages are not paid); the repair and lost sales are D03 and the insurance records of D09.

eventCatalog.name: A soaking rainy day
eventCatalog.text: Steady rain from morning to night. The passers-by are gone, the regulars still come, and the delivery tablet will not stop.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS forecast for New York City with rain through the day; Central Park daily precipitation of 0.5 inch or more
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 10 to 11 days with measurable precipitation in every month; two to four of them are all-day rains.
eventCatalog.note: 0.9 is the deck's rain value (measured sources listed in weatherDayEffects). The National Retail Federation's 2024 report notes that a missed daily coffee run is never made up later, so the loss is real, not shifted. Delivery +15% is the deck's value; the couriers are the limit. Hot drinks gain share on a cool wet day (-10% iced share is my estimate).

eventCatalog.name: A cold, late spring
eventCatalog.text: May feels like March. The parks are empty, the iced menu sits untouched, and people keep buying hot coffee the way they do in winter.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Monthly mean temperature at Central Park two or more degrees below the 1991-2020 normal (NWS monthly climate report)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: roughly one spring in three runs cooler than normal by this margin (my estimate from the definition of a normal).
eventCatalog.note: Planalytics with the National Retail Federation: weather swings coffee sales by 5% on average, and 'major markets in the Northeast can experience strong coffee demand of 10 percent above normal levels when cool weather extends into spring months'. +5% is half of that upper figure, for a whole month.

eventCatalog.name: Arctic blast
eventCatalog.text: The high today is 19 degrees. Nobody strolls. The ones who come in order the largest hot drink you sell and do not want to leave. Every time the door opens, the three tables next to it empty out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS Cold Weather Advisory for New York City; Central Park daily high at or below 25°F
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The 2025-26 winter was the coldest in 11 years in New York (CBS New York). January's normal high is 39.5°F and normal low 27.8°F.
eventCatalog.note: The deck's cold snap gives -5% foot traffic and +5% demand for cafes. Foursquare with AccuWeather found coffee shops lose traffic in extreme cold; 0.92 is my estimate. Heating +30% on those days is an estimate. The frozen-pipe risk belongs to D03.

eventCatalog.name: The clocks go back
eventCatalog.text: Sunset is at 4:50 now. The after-work walk-ins that carried your afternoons since March stop coming: people go straight home in the dark.
eventCatalog.realSignal: End of daylight saving time (November 1, 2026); sunset before 5 PM in New York from early November to late January
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year on the first Sunday of November.
eventCatalog.note: JPMorgan Chase Institute (2016, card data, Los Angeles against Phoenix, which does not change clocks): daily card spending per person falls 3.5% in the 30 days after the clocks go back; retail -4.8%, grocery -5.9%; Denver -4.9%, San Diego -2.2%. A cafe earns most of its day before noon, so I apply the loss to the afternoon half only: about -2.5%. The study covers 30 days; I extend it to two months as an estimate. Long evening hours (the existing hours lever) earn less in these months.

eventCatalog.name: Wind advisory
eventCatalog.text: Gusts of 50 miles an hour between the buildings. Your sandwich board is in the street, an umbrella is two doors down, and the awning is making a noise it should not make.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS Wind Advisory or High Wind Warning for New York City; Buildings Department weather advisory to secure sites
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Several advisories a year, mostly October to April.
eventCatalog.note: No measurement found; all values are estimates. The decision is what is outside: furniture and signs left out on an advisory day are the owner's liability if they hit someone (the same premises-liability logic as the fall claims).

eventCatalog.name: Smoke from Canada
eventCatalog.text: The sky is orange and the air smells like a campfire. The city tells people to stay inside. Your outdoor tables are empty, the door stays shut, and staff who bike to work are coughing.
eventCatalog.realSignal: EPA AirNow Air Quality Index for New York City at 151 or more; NYS Department of Environmental Conservation Air Quality Health Advisory
eventCatalog.realFrequency: June 6-8, 2023: index peaked at 465-484, the worst on record. July 16-19, 2026: peak 289, the second worst.
eventCatalog.note: The index figures are from NYC Emergency Management (July 19, 2026) and the Public Advocate's review of 2023. No sales figure was published for either event: in 2023 restaurant groups shut outdoor seating at a dozen places and some closed early. 0.8 is my estimate. With air_quality_plan = filters_and_masks the inside of the shop keeps its customers (apply 0.9 instead of 0.8) and staff availability stays at 1.

eventCatalog.name: Flash flood warning
eventCatalog.text: Two inches of rain in an hour. The street drains are fountains, the subway is suspended, and water is coming down your basement stairs toward the dry storage.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS Flash Flood Warning for New York (Manhattan, Kings or Queens) County; hourly rainfall at Central Park above 1.75 inches; NYC FloodNet street sensors; the city's Stormwater Flood Maps for the address

effects.onlyIf: flood_protection = none and the place has a basement in a mapped flood area
flood_protection = basic and the place has a basement in a mapped flood area

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the Comptroller's review of the September 29, 2023 storm: 'New York City's sewer system is only designed to manage 1.75 inches of rain' an hour; that morning peak rainfall 'exceeded 3 inches per hour in central and northern Brooklyn' and as much as 8.65 inches fell in the day; only 2.7% of New Yorkers over 16 got the city's emergency alert. Not opened: five storms above the limit in 2023 (DEP testimony) and 2.07 inches in one hour on July 14, 2025 (city release).
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic: the weather series gives the hour's rainfall, the place gives the basement and the flood-map flag, the lever gives the loss. After the September 2023 storm Brooklyn restaurants and bars reported equipment and produce destroyed and stock lost (Brownstoner); no dollar figures were published. $4,000 = dry goods, paper stock and a week of milk plus a cleanup crew; $600 = the insurance deductible share and labor with racks and a rider. Both are planning values. One closed day while the basement is pumped and sanitized.

eventCatalog.name: The floor drain runs backwards
eventCatalog.text: It is not even a big storm. The combined sewer under the street is full, and the lowest drain on the block is the one in your basement. What comes up is not rainwater.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Hourly rainfall near the sewer limit (1.5-1.75 inches); 311 sewer backup complaints for the block (open data, complaint type Sewer)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: DEP's own description: above the design rainfall 'the system would just back up until it could release itself, like a bathtub.'
eventCatalog.note: Happens to a shop with flood_protection = none on a block with past sewer complaints, in the first storm of the season near the limit. A shop that skips grease interceptor cleaning (existing shortcut) backs up at lower rainfall: its own line is already narrowed. Sewage in a food room means closing until it is cleaned and sanitized: one day and $2,500 are planning values. The backup rider pays the cleanup; the valve prevents it.

eventCatalog.name: Tropical storm watch
eventCatalog.text: A named storm is coming up the coast. The city tells shops to bring in everything loose, clear the catch basin, and expect the subway to stop running above ground.
eventCatalog.realSignal: National Hurricane Center Tropical Storm Watch or Warning for New York City; NYC Emergency Management coastal storm activation; MTA storm service plan
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: New York is brushed by a tropical system in some years and missed in most; the season runs June to November and peaks in September.
eventCatalog.note: All multipliers are estimates in line with the blizzard event. The game uses the watch and the two disrupted days only; it does not model loss of life or citywide destruction (rule 9). A roadway cafe platform must be secured or emptied; a storm outage is not reimbursed by Con Edison.

eventCatalog.name: Drought warning
eventCatalog.text: The reservoirs are at 60% when they should be near 80%. The city asks everyone to save water. If it becomes an emergency, hosing the sidewalk is banned and you serve water only when asked.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Department of Environmental Protection reservoir levels (published daily) and the drought stage: watch, warning, emergency
eventCatalog.realFrequency: November 18, 2024: the first drought warning in 22 years (a watch since November 2). The last warning, in early 2002, became an emergency three months later.
eventCatalog.note: No money effect at the warning stage: it is information and a reason to choose sweeping over hosing. At the emergency stage restaurants serve water on request only and washing sidewalks with a hose is restricted; the fine amounts were not found. The power-wash option of sidewalk_care should be unavailable during an emergency.

eventCatalog.name: Rat season
eventCatalog.text: Warm nights, full bins, and a block that puts out food waste three times a week. The rats are at their yearly peak, and the gap under your back door is half an inch.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 'Rodent' complaints for the community district (NYC Open Data, 311 Service Requests) and the Health Department's Rat Information Portal for the block
eventCatalog.realFrequency: My count of 311 'Rodent' complaints in 2025 by month: 2,180; 2,077; 2,896; 2,903; 3,332; 3,694; 3,635; 3,388; 2,785; 1,935; 1,354; 1,133 (31,312 in the year). June is 3.3 times December. Inside restaurants the season is reversed: citations for evidence of rats (code 04K) were highest in January (99) and December (91) and lowest in September (56).
eventCatalog.note: Both series are my queries of NYC Open Data (311 Service Requests; DOHMH Restaurant Inspection Results, inspections dated 2025). The 311 intake for rodent complaints was reported broken for part of late 2025, which may deepen the autumn drop. The event raises pressure; whether it becomes the existing pest_activity violation depends on three levers. Proposed rule (design): pressure 1 in June-September; +1 if trash is in bags or picked up three times a week; +1 if rodent_proofing = none; +1 if pest_control = none. At 3 or more the violation pest_activity is open from the next month. inspections x1.1 is an estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The building next door is coming down
eventCatalog.text: A demolition fence went up next door. When the old building goes, the rats that lived under it need a new address, and yours is the nearest kitchen.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Buildings Department demolition and new-building permits for adjacent lots (DOB NOW open data), which must carry a rodent-extermination certification
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: thousands of demolition permits are issued in the city each year; the count was not confirmed in this session.
eventCatalog.note: Local Law 109 of 2022: an applicant for full demolition, or demolition of more than half a building, must certify that a licensed exterminator treats the site before the permit is issued; a 2023 law extended this to most new construction. The treatment is a permit condition, not a guarantee. Demolition displaces rats by destroying burrows and by vibration. Same pressure rule as the summer peak, +1 for six months. Dust and a sidewalk shed on the neighbor's lot take 3% of traffic (estimate).

eventCatalog.name: Cold weather: the mice come inside
eventCatalog.text: The first frost sends every mouse on the block looking for warmth. Your wall backs onto a hundred-year-old basement. Droppings behind the pastry case are a critical violation.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Daily lows under 40°F at Central Park from late October; the monthly count of code 04L in the DOHMH restaurant inspection data
eventCatalog.realFrequency: My count of citations for evidence of mice (code 04L) in 2025 restaurant inspections by month: 425; 284; 348; 338; 288; 289; 295; 291; 320; 364; 344; 413. Measured against a steady citation (10F) as a stand-in for the number of inspections, the rate is lowest in July (0.27) and highest in January (0.44): 60% higher.
eventCatalog.note: Query of NYC Open Data 'DOHMH New York City Restaurant Inspection Results': inspections dated in 2025, grouped by month and violation code. The data set holds only establishments that are active now, and the 10F ratio is my proxy for inspection volume, so read the shape, not the level. The season runs from October through January, longer than the two months of the first pass. Uses the rodent pressure rule.

eventCatalog.name: Flies
eventCatalog.text: A cloud of tiny flies over the syrup pumps and the floor drain. Milk residue, warm weather and a drain nobody scrubs. An inspector counts flies as a critical violation.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The monthly count of code 04N in the DOHMH restaurant inspection data; daily highs above 75°F; follows from cleaning = minimal
eventCatalog.realFrequency: My count of citations for filth flies (code 04N) in 2025 restaurant inspections by month: 141; 64; 100; 118; 133; 206; 366; 397; 388; 438; 351; 253. Against the same stand-in for inspection volume the rate is 0.07 in February and 0.34-0.40 from July through October: about five times higher. The peak is October, not July.
eventCatalog.note: Query of NYC Open Data, as for the mice event. Health Department code 04N covers filth flies and is scored like the other pest items in the pack's inspectionPoints table. The event adds no new fine: with cleaning = minimal it opens the existing dirty_surfaces and pest_activity trails from June to November. Roaches (04M) follow the same season: 55 citations in February, 175 in August. The quality effect is a design value.

eventCatalog.name: No pickup for a week
eventCatalog.text: The plows come first. Collection is running days behind, the bins are full, and bags are stacked on the snowbank in front of your window.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DSNY collection-delay notices after a Snow Alert; the private carter's service messages
eventCatalog.realFrequency: After the January 25 and February 22, 2026 storms: city collection ran about 24 hours behind and then days behind; regular collection resumed citywide on February 26.
eventCatalog.note: The reports are about city (residential) collection; nothing was found on private carters in those weeks, so the effect on a business is my assumption that carters were delayed the same way. Daily pickup buys nothing in that week. The quality effect is a design value; the real risk is the rodent pressure rule (+1 for the month).

eventCatalog.name: Outdoor season
eventCatalog.text: The first evenings above 60 degrees. Every table on the sidewalk is taken, and the shops without tables watch people walk past to the ones that have them.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Daily highs between 60°F and 85°F with no rain (NWS forecast); the Dining Out NYC season calendar
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year; under the 2026 law licensed roadway setups no longer have to come down on November 30.
eventCatalog.note: Mechanic outdoor_seat_days counts the usable days. The deck's card gives every cafe +4% demand for two weeks from April 1; it should apply only to shops with licensed outdoor seats (or with the existing sidewalk_tables shortcut, at the price of the violation). Opened NYC311: 'Sidewalk setups are allowed year-round'; the Council passed year-round roadway dining, with applications opening in early September 2026 and 'a year-round license with higher fees'; license fee $1,050 for four years, or $2,100 for roadway and sidewalk together.

eventCatalog.name: Keep the roadway cafe up this winter?
eventCatalog.text: For the first time since the pandemic you may keep your roadway cafe through the winter. The rules for winter-proofing and snow are not written yet, the heaters must be electric, and the plow does not go around you.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC DOT Dining Out NYC rulemaking notices (rules.cityofnewyork.us) on winterization and snow removal; DSNY Snow Alerts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New in 2026: Intro 655-A, signed August 31, 2026, with a one-year interim license for existing setups.
eventCatalog.note: Winter use of 20% of the seats and +3% utilities for electric heaters are my estimates. Propane heaters are not allowed: the Fire Department's pandemic exception ended in 2021; electric heaters are allowed on sidewalks and roadways. The alternative is the seasonal license: take the platform down (removal and storage were reported at several thousand dollars a year under the old rule; no figure was confirmed here).

eventCatalog.name: January
eventCatalog.text: The holidays are over, the credit card bills are in, half your regulars gave up sugar and the other half are working from home because it is 28 degrees. This is the slowest month of the coffee year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Calendar; card-spending panels for coffee chains (Bloomberg Second Measure); office-visit indexes in the first two weeks of January
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year.
eventCatalog.note: Card-panel analysis of Starbucks: January is its lowest-sales month of the year; in 2016 its December sales ran 58% above January's and 14% above November's. A neighborhood shop does not have Starbucks' holiday gift-card peak, so I take a much smaller swing: -8% against an average month. Plan cash for it in December: January also brings the minimum-wage step and annual renewals.

eventCatalog.name: August: the offices empty out
eventCatalog.text: Half of every team is on vacation and the other half has Summer Fridays. The lunch line at the towers is short, and on Friday afternoon you could close at two.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai monthly office index and Kastle Back to Work Barometer for the New York metro; MTA weekday subway ridership (data.ny.gov)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. Nationwide office visits were 34.3% below 2019 in August 2025 against 21.8% below in July.
eventCatalog.note: (1 - 0.343) / (1 - 0.218) = 0.84 of July. National index; New York recovers better than most cities (June 2025: 5.3% below 2019) but follows the same season. Applies to places whose footfall is mostly office workers; a residential or tourist block uses the other August events.

eventCatalog.name: Summer weekends: the neighborhood leaves town
eventCatalog.text: From Memorial Day to Labor Day your Saturday regulars are at the beach, upstate or at their in-laws'. The brunch line that carried your spring is a third shorter.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Calendar (Memorial Day to Labor Day); weekend subway entries at the nearest stations; school recess dates
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every summer. NYC Hospitality Alliance survey: 72% of restaurants reported lower sales in June-August 2024 than a year before; of those, 43% were down 1-10%, 29% down 11-20% and 24% down 21-30%.
eventCatalog.note: The survey compares one summer with the previous one, not summer with spring, so it shows how common a weak summer is, not the size of the seasonal dip. No published monthly index for independent New York cafes was found. -18% on weekend days in July-August for a residential block is my estimate; month value 8 days x 18% / 30 = 5%.

eventCatalog.name: School is back
eventCatalog.text: September 10: nine hundred thousand children go back to school. The 8 AM drop-off crowd returns to your door, offices fill up again, and the city remembers its routine.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Public Schools calendar: first day Thursday, September 10, 2026; office-visit indexes after Labor Day
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year.
eventCatalog.note: The date is official. +5% for September-October against the yearly average is my estimate: Placer.ai describes fall routines and return-to-office mandates lifting office visits each autumn, and chains post their best months in October-December.

eventCatalog.name: School recess week
eventCatalog.text: No school this week. The stroller parade is gone, families with money are away, and the teenagers who are left sit for three hours over one hot chocolate.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Public Schools calendar: December 24-January 1, February 15-19 and April 22-30 in the 2026-27 year
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Three recess weeks a year plus the summer.
eventCatalog.note: Dates are official; the 10% drop on recess weekdays is my estimate. Tourist districts move the other way in the same weeks (out-of-town families).

eventCatalog.name: The week between Christmas and New Year's
eventCatalog.text: Offices are dark from the 24th to the 2nd. Midtown belongs to tourists, the residential blocks to people in sweatpants at eleven in the morning, and the towers to nobody.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Calendar; December office index (33.1% below 2019 in December 2025); hotel occupancy

effects.onlyIf: place is in a tourist district

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year.
eventCatalog.note: Placer.ai's December 2025 index: office visits 33.1% below 2019, 'tis the season to work from home'. Month values: office district -10% (the last third of the month nearly empty), tourist district +5% (estimate; monthly hotel occupancy for New York was not found). Schools are closed December 24, 2026-January 1, 2027.

eventCatalog.name: The students go home
eventCatalog.text: Commencement was last week. The laptops, the group projects and the 11 PM study crowd are gone until September, and with them a third of your sales.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Academic calendars of the nearest university (last day of exams, commencement, first day of fall classes)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every summer, and a shorter dip from mid-December to late January.
eventCatalog.note: Qualitative only: coverage of Morningside Heights describes bars and coffee shops that 'work in an ecosystem with the university community'; owners in other college towns say trade 'drops drastically' when students leave. No New York figure was found. The engine's place model already takes 12% off a campus block in summer; -25% is my estimate for a shop whose customers are mostly students. The right number is a calibration question for D06.

eventCatalog.name: Finals
eventCatalog.text: Every seat is taken by nine in the morning and nobody leaves. Sales per seat fall while the room looks full: one cold brew buys four hours of table.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University exam calendars (first half of May, mid-December)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Twice a year.
eventCatalog.note: Design values, no measurement. The point for the sizing model: demand rises but seats turn over more slowly, so a small room hits the crowd penalty. Time limits and laptop-free tables are D02 levers.

eventCatalog.name: Tourist high season
eventCatalog.text: Hotel rooms are full and the sidewalks near the sights are shoulder to shoulder. Visitors do not know your shop: they walk into the first door with a line or a logo they recognize.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Tourism + Conventions visitor counts and forecasts; hotel occupancy reports

effects.onlyIf: place is in a tourist district

eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 65 million visitors in 2025 (+0.7%); the forecast for 2026 was 66.3 million. International visitors fell 3.2% in 2025 to 12.5 million, still below 13.5 million in 2019.
eventCatalog.note: The deck's value (+8% in prime locations in June-August). Visitor totals are NYC Tourism + Conventions figures quoted by web search. A month-by-month occupancy series was not found, so the choice of months is my reading: summer and the weeks from Thanksgiving to New Year's.

eventCatalog.name: January and February: no visitors
eventCatalog.text: The tree is down and the hotels are half price. Blocks that live on visitors feel it first.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Hotel occupancy and average room rates for New York City; NYC Tourism winter promotions (Restaurant Week, Broadway Week, Hotel Week)

effects.onlyIf: place is in a tourist district

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year; the city schedules its discount weeks in exactly these months.
eventCatalog.note: The existence of Restaurant Week (January 19-February 11 in 2027) is the evidence that these are the slow weeks; the -10% is my estimate, no occupancy series was found.

eventCatalog.name: Pumpkin spice comes back
eventCatalog.text: The chains launched their fall menus today, in August heat. Starbucks just had its biggest Tuesday of the year, and some of that line would have been yours.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain menu launch dates (Starbucks: August 25, 2026; Dunkin': August 19, 2026); Placer.ai visit counts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year, a little earlier each time.
eventCatalog.note: Placer.ai: Starbucks visits on August 25, 2026 were 25.7% above its daily average for the year and 35.1% above an average Tuesday; in 2025 the pumpkin menu lifted its traffic 11.3-15.9% in the three days after launch. For an independent the effect is small and its sign depends on the menu: -1% with nothing seasonal, +2% with a fall special of its own (my estimates).

eventCatalog.name: Small Business Saturday
eventCatalog.text: The Saturday after Thanksgiving. The neighborhood association hands out maps, and people who usually order online make a point of walking the block.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Calendar: the Saturday after Thanksgiving (November 28, 2026); the local business improvement district's program
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year since 2010. Shoppers reported spending about $22 billion at small businesses on the day in 2024 (American Express survey cited by the Small Business Administration).
eventCatalog.note: The $22 billion is self-reported by consumers, not receipts. +10% on the day for a cafe on a shopping block is my estimate; over the month it is a third of a percent, so no month effect is set. Bags of beans and gift cards sell that day.

eventCatalog.name: Thanksgiving parade at your corner
eventCatalog.text: People have been standing on the avenue since 6 AM in the cold. They want coffee, cocoa and a bathroom. You are behind a police barrier, and your delivery is not coming.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Parade route and NYPD street closures for Thanksgiving morning (November 26, 2026): Central Park West, Sixth Avenue, 34th Street
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year, on the route only.
eventCatalog.note: All multipliers are my estimates. Double traffic for about five hours; a shop that chose holiday_hours = closed gets nothing. Capacity, not demand, is the limit: the window menu option is the move. The seats_20 bathroom rule matters on this day more than any other.

eventCatalog.name: Pride Sunday
eventCatalog.text: Two million people between Chelsea and the Village. If you are on the route, it is the biggest day of your year and the hardest to staff: nobody can get across Fifth Avenue.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Pride March route and NYPD closures, last Sunday of June (June 28, 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year; Fifth Avenue, Greenwich Village and Chelsea.
eventCatalog.note: The deck has +10% in prime locations citywide; on the route the day is different. Multipliers are my estimates; the crowd figure is the organizers' usual claim and was not checked. Trash doubles: the sidewalk in front is still yours to clean by the next routing hour.

eventCatalog.name: A parade closes your avenue
eventCatalog.text: Barriers line the curb from nine to four. Your regulars from across the avenue cannot cross. The people on your side are here for the parade, not for you.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Street Activity Permit Office parade permits ('NYC Permitted Event Information' open data): St. Patrick's Day (March 17), Puerto Rican Day (June 14, 2026), West Indian Day (September 7, 2026), Columbus Day (October 12)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Fifth Avenue hosts a dozen parades a year; Eastern Parkway one very large one.
eventCatalog.note: Estimates. The logic is the same as the street fair and the marathon: more people, lower conversion, no deliveries. Which side of the barrier your regulars live on decides the day.

eventCatalog.name: Sunday race: streets closed until noon
eventCatalog.text: Thirty thousand cyclists come through at 8 AM. The avenue is closed from 6 to 12, right through your Sunday rush, and the staff who drive in are stuck on the wrong side.
eventCatalog.realSignal: City street-closure notices for the NYC Half (March 15, 2026) and the Five Boro Bike Tour (first Sunday of May)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Two Sunday mornings a year on the routes.
eventCatalog.note: Riders and runners do not stop; spectators are few. -15% on the morning is my estimate. The bike tour date is from memory.

eventCatalog.name: UN General Assembly week
eventCatalog.text: Motorcades, concrete blocks and checkpoints from 42nd to 57th Street. Cars move at walking speed. Your regulars work from home this week, and the delegates are fed inside their hotels.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYPD street closures for the General Assembly's high-level week (late September); DOT Gridlock Alert Days
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every September. In 2025 Midtown traffic ran below 5 mph, the slowest of the year.
eventCatalog.note: A corner-store owner near the UN in 2025: 'When there is a road closure, I lose business... My regular customers, they avoid coming outside', and visitors did not make up for it. Local reports in 2026 again describe fewer customers near the blockades. No figure exists; -20% on five days inside the security zone is my estimate. The deck models only delivery and staffing.

eventCatalog.name: New Year's Eve: inside the frozen zone
eventCatalog.text: From four in the afternoon the blocks from Sixth to Eighth Avenue, 42nd to 57th Street, are closed to everyone but emergency vehicles. Anyone coming to your door needs a police officer to let them through.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYPD and Times Square Alliance New Year's Eve closure plan and business guidance, published each December

effects.onlyIf: place is in the Times Square zone

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once a year, Times Square area only.
eventCatalog.note: The Times Square Alliance's guidance for businesses, as quoted by web search: police may freeze blocks, guests should arrive early, and a business needs a representative at the nearest corner on Sixth or Eighth Avenue to identify its guests to the officer. The 2025 closure began at 4:00 PM. Multipliers are my estimates: the morning is normal, the afternoon and night are lost unless you sell to the people already penned in.

eventCatalog.name: World Cup summer
eventCatalog.text: Eight matches across the river and a million visitors in the region. The bars with screens are full. A cafe without one gets the traffic warnings, the closed streets and the late deliveries.
eventCatalog.realSignal: FIFA match schedule for the New York New Jersey stadium (June 13-July 19, 2026); city fan-zone street closures; gridlock alerts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once: summer 2026.
eventCatalog.note: Correction to the deck (+8% foot traffic and +5% demand for cafes). What was measured afterwards: the city estimated a $2 billion impact and said foot traffic at sports bars rose 16% over the year before, part of it from the Knicks' Finals run. A PYMNTS survey of small businesses in host cities: 43% reported higher summer sales, and only 29% of those credited the tournament; venues that did not show matches were more likely to report lower sales, citing street closures and delivery problems. +2% in prime locations is my reading for a cafe.

eventCatalog.name: Commuter rail strike
eventCatalog.text: The Long Island Rail Road is shut. A quarter of a million daily riders are told to work from home, and the concourse where your morning line forms is empty.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Union strike deadlines under the Railway Labor Act; MTA and NJ Transit service notices

effects.onlyIf: place is near Penn Station, Grand Central or Atlantic Terminal
place is near a commuter rail terminal

eventCatalog.realFrequency: May 16, 2026: about 3,500 Long Island Rail Road workers walked out, the first strike there in 32 years, on a system with 250,000 daily commuters. NJ Transit engineers struck for three days in May 2025.
eventCatalog.note: The strike deadline is public weeks ahead, which fits the no-dice rule: the event is announced. On the first Saturday reporters counted a few dozen people in the main concourse of Penn Station. -40% on strike weekdays for a terminal-dependent shop is my estimate; how long the 2026 strike lasted was not confirmed in this session, four working days is a placeholder.

eventCatalog.name: Ramadan: the day goes quiet, the night comes alive
eventCatalog.text: For a month your neighbors do not eat or drink until sunset. Lunch is slow. After the evening prayer the block fills up, and the cafes that stay open until three have a line out the door.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The Islamic calendar: Ramadan ran from about February 18 to March 19 in 2026 and moves about 11 days earlier each year; sunset times

effects.onlyIf: place is in a neighborhood with many Muslim residents

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year; strongest in Bay Ridge, Astoria, Jackson Heights and parts of the Bronx.
eventCatalog.note: Reporting on Yemeni coffeehouses (public radio, March 2026; Associated Press, May 2026): they stay open past 3 AM during Ramadan and fill after the night prayers; a Bay Ridge branch was 'overflowing well past 11 p.m.' No sales figures. -20% for a shop that keeps daytime hours and +10% for one that opens late are my estimates. The existing long-hours option ends at 9 PM; this event needs a later one.

eventCatalog.name: The Jewish holidays
eventCatalog.text: On Yom Kippur the avenue is silent. In Passover week the regulars who keep the holiday do not buy your croissants, and many families are away.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The Hebrew calendar: Rosh Hashanah September 11-13 and Yom Kippur September 20-21 in 2026 (public schools closed September 21); Passover in April

effects.onlyIf: place is in a neighborhood with many observant Jewish residents

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year; strongest in parts of Brooklyn, the Upper West Side and Riverdale.
eventCatalog.note: Only the school closure is sourced. The -3% of a month is my estimate (two or three near-empty days, a slow pastry week). Included because an owner new to a neighborhood finds it out in the first September.

eventCatalog.name: Lunar New Year
eventCatalog.text: Firecrackers, a lion dance going shop to shop, and a parade that fills the street for a day. Family-run suppliers close for the week, so order early.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The lunar calendar (February 17, 2026; February 6, 2027); parade permits for Chinatown, Flushing and Sunset Park; public schools close for the day

effects.onlyIf: place is in Chinatown, Flushing or Sunset Park

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year.
eventCatalog.note: Estimates; the 2027 date is from memory. The non-obvious part is supply: small produce and bakery wholesalers in those neighborhoods close for several days.

eventCatalog.name: People stay home
eventCatalog.text: After a week of immigration arrests in the news, the avenue is half empty. Customers send one person to shop for three families. Two of your staff ask to change their shifts.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Federal enforcement operations reported in the city; surveys by local merchant associations and business improvement districts; mobile-phone foot-traffic panels

effects.onlyIf: place is in a neighborhood with many immigrant residents

eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2025-2026. A survey of 30 businesses in Flatbush (August 2026): 70% reported a drop in foot traffic and 90% higher costs; the group itself says the survey does not prove the cause. A working paper on the first year of the current administration measured 2.9% less foot traffic and 6.9% less spending in affected areas.
eventCatalog.note: Stated neutrally and scoped to what was measured. -5% of foot traffic sits between the working paper (2.9% traffic, 6.9% spending) and owner reports of much larger drops on single avenues. Staff effect is my estimate. The event carries no judgement and no enforcement mechanic for the player; it is a demand shock like a closed station.

eventCatalog.name: Corner shop: twice the snow
eventCatalog.text: You pay extra rent for two windows. After a snowfall you also own two sidewalks, two curb ramps, the hydrant and the slush pond at the crosswalk.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Place data: corner lot (two frontages); the same snow days as snowfall_clear_the_walk

effects.onlyIf: place is a corner lot and snow_ice_plan = staff_shovel

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every snowfall, for corner places only.
eventCatalog.note: Opened NYC311: 'Clear access to the crosswalk and pedestrian ramp (curb cut) if you own a corner property. Shovel bus stops (without shelters) and fire hydrants.' The engine's place model already gives a corner a 25% visibility bonus; this is its winter cost: staff time doubles ($30 more per snowfall, see the lever note), and an uncleared ramp is a separate reason for a 311 complaint.

eventCatalog.name: The milk truck does not come
eventCatalog.text: Your dairy and pastry deliveries are cancelled for the storm. The shops that ordered a day ahead have croissants. You have filter coffee and apologies.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Supplier service notices before a Winter Storm Warning; NYC Emergency Management travel advisories

effects.onlyIf: no extra order placed before the storm

eventCatalog.realFrequency: With each warned storm: two in the 2025-26 winter.
eventCatalog.note: Estimate: with no pastry and short milk a cafe sells about 15% less on the days the street is passable again. The delivery platforms themselves suspend service in the worst hours (DoorDash severe weather protocol, January 2026). The move is ordering ahead when the warning is issued, which the storm_day_policy lever should include as a paid option (one extra day of stock, some of it wasted).

eventCatalog.name: Manhole fire: the block goes dark
eventCatalog.text: Salt and meltwater have been dripping onto hundred-year-old cables under the street for a week. This morning a manhole cover is smoking, the Fire Department has closed the block, and Con Edison has cut the power.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Con Edison outage map; Fire Department manhole incident reports; the days after a salted snowfall followed by a thaw
eventCatalog.realFrequency: In 2014, 68% of the city's manhole events happened in January and February; one winter saw about 550 manhole fires in a few weeks. Con Edison says events have declined since 2015 as it replaces old cable.
eventCatalog.note: No dice: the world schedules a fixed small number of these per winter on blocks with the oldest underground network, two to five days after a salted storm. One closed day = 3% of a month. $400 = milk and food lost without ice chests (planning value). An outage of more than 12 hours caused by Con Edison's equipment allows a spoilage claim of up to $12,900 (opened NYC311), but not when a storm caused it.

eventCatalog.name: A pipe bursts overnight
eventCatalog.text: Eleven degrees at 4 AM, the heat was turned down to save money, and the supply line in the back wall froze. You open the door to an inch of water and a ceiling tile on the espresso machine.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Not a public signal: follows from winter_proofing = none on the first night with a low at or below 15°F at Central Park
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: water and freezing damage is 20% of small-business insurance claims and averages $34,600 (The Hartford, 2025; $17,000 in 2015).
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic: only for a shop that chose none, at most once a winter. $2,500 = deductible and uninsured losses (planning value); three closed days and a 15% premium increase are my estimates. The 15°F threshold is a design value. The insurer pays the $34,600; the owner pays the closed days. Opened the Insurance Journal report of The Hartford's analysis: water and freezing damage 'represented approximately 22% of small-business claims over the past five years, averaging $34,600 per claim', 20% of claims in 2025; slip, fall and customer injury rose from 10% to 20% of claims and from $20,000 to $45,000; burglary and theft 20%; fire $80,000.

eventCatalog.name: Nobody queues in the cold
eventCatalog.text: In October a line out the door is an advertisement. In January people look at it through the window and keep walking. Whatever does not fit inside your door is lost.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Daily high at or below 35°F; place data: floor space for a queue inside the door
eventCatalog.realFrequency: December to February: January's normal high is 39.5°F.
eventCatalog.note: No measurement found; the -3% of capacity is a design value. The mechanic belongs to D02 (queue space) and D06 (queue walk-away); the winter condition is the D07 part: the same six-person queue that works in May fails in January unless it is indoors. Mobile order-ahead and a second register are the real answers.

eventCatalog.name: The cellar doors are open again
eventCatalog.text: The paper-goods driver propped the sidewalk hatch open and went back to the truck. A woman looking at her phone stops one step from the hole.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Place data: sidewalk cellar doors; delivery schedule
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every delivery day in the many old buildings whose only route to the basement is through the sidewalk.
eventCatalog.note: Creates no cost by itself; with delivery_hatch_rule = open_and_go for six months it raises one cellar_hatch_fall_claim (extra.claims). Restaurant insurance brokers list open cellar doors among the main sources of sidewalk claims in New York.

eventCatalog.name: A lake at your corner
eventCatalog.text: Leaves and a pizza box are blocking the storm drain. After every rain there is an ankle-deep pond at the curb, exactly where people cross to reach your door.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 'catch basin clogged or flooding' complaints for the intersection (NYC Open Data); leaf fall and snowmelt
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: common in leaf season and during snowmelt.
eventCatalog.note: The basin belongs to the Department of Environmental Protection, but the 18 inches of gutter in front of it are yours to keep clean, and DSNY asks owners to clear basins after snow. The -1% is a design value for a shop that never sweeps the gutter.

eventCatalog.name: Your commercial waste zone goes live
eventCatalog.text: The city has divided itself into 20 waste zones with a short list of authorized carters in each. Your zone starts now: your old hauler may not be on the list, and you have two months to sign a new contract or the city picks a carter for you.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DSNY Commercial Waste Zones rollout schedule and the final rules that set each zone's start and transition dates
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the DSNY final rule of June 2026. Implementation start and final dates: Bronx East and Bronx West, October 1-November 30, 2025; Queens Northeast and Brooklyn South, January 1-February 28, 2026; Lower Manhattan, April 1-May 31, 2026; Midtown South and Staten Island, July 1-August 31, 2026; Brooklyn North and Upper Manhattan, October 1-November 30, 2026. Queens Central was first: September 3, 2024-January 2, 2025 (NYC311). Later rules set the remaining zones.
eventCatalog.note: Each zone gets a two-month window between its start and final implementation dates. Opened NYC311: 'Businesses must sign a new service agreement with a zone-authorized carter when their zone is rolled out... If businesses in that zone fail to do so, DSNY will select a carter for that business.' No money effect is set: each authorized carter has a maximum-rate table and the customer may negotiate below it; no independent price comparison was found.

eventCatalog.name: City Hall reviews small-business fines
eventCatalog.text: The mayor has ordered every agency to list the rules and fines that fall on small businesses and to propose which to cut, soften or replace with a warning. Nothing changes until an agency rewrites its rule.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Executive Order 11 (January 14, 2026) and the agency reports it requires; the July 2026 OPEN for Small Business package; rule changes published at rules.cityofnewyork.us
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Opened the Comptroller's review (2026): the 2022 Small Business Forward round evaluated 232 regulations and recommended changes to 116; only 36 of those 116 were regularly used to issue violations. Executive Order 11 of January 14, 2026, 'Reducing Fees and Civil Penalties for Small Business', is the third round.
eventCatalog.note: Information only, like the regulation cards in the deck. Matters for this pack because several fines in it (sidewalk, trash, signs) are the kind the review targets: the mayor campaigned on halving fines and fees, and the order asks for an amnesty study within a year. An April 2026 Comptroller review found that nobody had measured the effect of the earlier cuts. Fines in this fragment are the amounts in force when checked.

eventCatalog.name: The neighbors upstairs call 311
eventCatalog.text: Windows are open in May. The family on the second floor can hear your playlist, your grinder at 6:30 and your exhaust fan all day. An inspector with a sound meter is coming to their living room.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 'Noise - Commercial' complaints for the address (NYC Open Data, 311 Service Requests)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: OATH hearings data, violations since January 1, 2025: 48 first-offense cases of music from a commercial establishment over permitted levels ($2,000; $8,000 on default; $0 in 4 cured cases) and 65 for unreasonable noise from a sound device ($440; $1,750 on default).
eventCatalog.note: Opens the commercial_music_noise violation only for a shop with the speaker shortcut on or with long hours in a building with apartments above. The first violation costs nothing if cured: turn it down, move the speaker, put the grinder on a mat. Few cases reach a summons; most complaints end with a visit.

eventCatalog.name: Break-in
eventCatalog.text: The glass in the door is on the floor and the register drawer is gone with the $200 float. The police take a report. The glazier can come Thursday.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYPD CompStat burglary counts for the precinct (weekly PDF and the NYPD complaint data on NYC Open Data); follows from night_security = lock_only
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Burglaries citywide were down 19.2% for the year to mid-May 2026, the lowest on record; February 2026 had 784 against 977 a year before. Burglary and theft are still 20% of small-business insurance claims.
eventCatalog.note: No dice: the world assigns a fixed number of break-ins per year from the precinct's real count to businesses with lock_only, oldest lease first; a shop with gate_and_alarm is skipped. $1,500 = a tempered-glass door panel, the float and the deductible share (planning value). CompStat does not separate commercial from residential burglary.

eventCatalog.name: A holiday market opens across the square
eventCatalog.text: A hundred wooden stalls, six weeks, and a hot-chocolate kiosk every thirty feet. The square has never been so full, and never had so many places to buy a hot drink.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Parks Department and market operator calendars: Union Square, Bryant Park and Columbus Circle markets run from late October or mid-November to late December

effects.onlyIf: place is within two blocks of a holiday market

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year at the same squares.
eventCatalog.note: The deck's holiday-market card gives prime locations +8% foot traffic; the catch is competition from the stalls, the same logic as the street fair. The -3% without a seasonal drink is my estimate. A warm room with seats is the one thing the stalls do not have.

eventCatalog.name: The tables by the door are empty
eventCatalog.text: Every customer who walks in brings a blast of 25-degree air with them. Nobody sits at the three tables nearest the door, and the heater runs all day to replace what the door lets out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Daily high at or below 40°F (normal highs: December 44.4°F, January 39.5°F, February 42.2°F); place data: door opens directly into the seating area
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every winter in a storefront with a single door and no lobby.
eventCatalog.note: No measurement found: 15% of seats lost on cold days and 6% more heating are design values. The legal fix is the seasonal storm enclosure (see the lever note for the rule as a vendor describes it). An air curtain is the other option and a D03 equipment item.

eventCatalog.name: The city marks your sidewalk
eventCatalog.text: An inspector spray-painted the cracked flags in front of your door and mailed the owner a violation. The owner forwarded it to you with one line: see clause 14 of your lease.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC DOT sidewalk inspections and violations (open data: 'Sidewalk Management Database - Violations'); 311 sidewalk condition complaints for the address

effects.onlyIf: lease makes the tenant repair the sidewalk

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reference only: DOT inspects after complaints and before its own repair contracts; the yearly count of violations was not confirmed in this session.
