eventCatalog.note: Opened NYC311: 'If sidewalk defects are not repaired within 75 days after a Sidewalk Violation Notice was issued, DOT may perform the work and bill you for the repair'; 'There is no fine or penalty associated with the violation'; defects from tree roots next to commercial buildings are the owner's responsibility. $2,400 = four concrete flags (100 square feet) at about $24 a square foot with permit, my planning value. The cost lands on the tenant only where the lease says so. A marked defect that nobody fixed is also evidence in a trip-and-fall claim.

eventCatalog.name: A perfect Saturday
eventCatalog.text: Seventy-two degrees and not a cloud. The whole neighborhood is in the park with a blanket. If you are on the way to the park gate you sell out of cold brew by noon. If you are four blocks the other way, your room is empty.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS forecast: dry weekend day with a high between 65°F and 82°F; place data: distance to a large park entrance

effects.onlyIf: place is within two blocks of a large park entrance
place is residential and not near a park

eventCatalog.realFrequency: About four such weekend days a month in May, June, September and October.
eventCatalog.note: The engine's place model already gives a shop near a park +10% on warm weekends; this adds the other side (people leave the indoor rooms) and the takeaway shift: fewer seats used, more cups carried out. All values are estimates.

mechanics.title: The sidewalk is yours: a legal clock after every snowfall
mechanics.playerDecision: A standing order for December-March (lever snow_ice_plan): staff shovel on the clock, a seasonal contractor, or nothing. On a blizzard day a second order (storm_day_policy): open with a skeleton crew or close.
mechanics.engineMath: The weather series already marks snow days. For each snow day d the engine sets a deadline from the hour the snow stopped (weather seed gives the hour; daytime 7:00-16:59 -> d + 4 h; 17:00-20:59 -> + 14 h; overnight -> 11:00 next morning). staff_shovel: cost = 1.5 h x wage + $5 ice melt per snow day, and one worker is off the bar for that time (capacity that hour -1). contractor: flat monthly fee, no capacity loss. none: (1) violation snow_ice_not_cleared is open from the deadline until the ice is gone (snow depth 0 or three days above freezing): any sanitation inspection or 311 complaint in that window finds it; every uncleared snowfall is a new $100 summons, and a summons left unanswered (the default answer of an absent player must be to pay) becomes $350; (2) footTraffic at this door x 0.85 on those days; (3) the first such window of the winter creates one sidewalk_fall_claim that lands 60-120 days later. No dice: every branch follows from the weather series and the order.

mechanics.title: Temperature moves the mix, not the count: hot against iced
mechanics.playerDecision: Before the warm months: size the ice machine and stock cold cups (setup and supplies), choose the seasonal menu lever, and set a price for iced drinks. In a heat wave: the cooling plan.
mechanics.engineMath: Each day: icedShare = clamp(0.20 + 0.0122 x (highF - 59) + 0.15, 0.10, 0.80), times event multipliers (rain 0.9, heat 1.1). Orders split into hot and iced. Iced orders use the iced unit cost and price (D04 supplies both; here the placeholder is +1% on cost of goods in iced-heavy months) and draw ice: icedOrders x 0.4 lb against the machine's daily output; orders beyond the ice are lost unless the player buys bagged ice (cash cost). Total orders move only through footTraffic and the weatherDayEffects table. A month's report shows the split so the player learns why July margins differ from January's.

mechanics.title: The basement is cheap storage until it rains two inches in an hour
mechanics.playerDecision: At lease signing the player sees whether the address has a basement and whether the city's stormwater flood map shades the block. Then a standing order: flood_protection none, basic or full.
mechanics.engineMath: The weather series carries the peak hourly rainfall of each wet day. If peakHourly >= the block's sewer limit (1.75 in, or 1.5 in in most of Queens) and the place is in a mapped flood area with a basement: none -> lose basementStockValue (default 40% of inventory) + cleanup, one closed day; basic -> deductible and labor only; full -> nothing. Blocks outside the map are not flooded by this rule. A separate, smaller rule fires sewer_backup at 85% of the limit for shops with none, and at 70% for shops that also skip grease-interceptor cleaning. All thresholds are fixed numbers, so the same rain gives the same result for every player.

mechanics.title: Trash, season and neighbors add up to a rodent score
mechanics.playerDecision: Three standing orders that interact: trash_setup (bins and pickups), rodent_proofing, and the existing pest_control lever.
mechanics.engineMath: pressure = season (1 in June-September for rats outdoors and flies, 1 in October-January for mice and rats indoors, else 0) + neighbors (1 while demolition_next_door or trash_piles_after_snow is active) + trash (1 if the shortcut bags_on_curb is on, 1 for three pickups in June-September, 0 for daily pickup) + proofing (1 if rodent_proofing = none) + extermination (1 if pest_control = none). At pressure >= 3 the existing violation pest_activity is open from the first day of the next month and stays open until pressure has been below 3 for a full month. No dice. The player sees the score and its parts in the risk panel, so the fix is always visible.

extra.howNumbersWereChecked: Two passes on November 14, 2026. First pass: web search only, because the cloud environment refused every outside host; numbers from that pass are 'estimate' with evidence 'official_excerpt' (search quoted the official page named in source), 'secondary' (news, trade press, vendor or insurer report) or 'calc' (my arithmetic or a design value, shown in note). Second pass, after the owner allowed 20 hosts: I downloaded the pages and data myself. Numbers I saw there are 'verified' with evidence 'opened_official' (agency page, law-making document or official PDF) or 'open_data_query' (my own count from NYC Open Data, query described in note). 'secondary_opened' = a trade-press page I opened that reports someone else's study; it stays 'estimate'. Not reachable even after access: www.nyc.gov, www.nycourts.gov and codelibrary.amlegal.com answer automated requests with 403 from their own bot protection, and I did not work around that; everything sourced only to those three hosts is still 'official_excerpt'. Game-balance values (multipliers, quality effects, reputation hits) are design choices, not facts.

claims.name: Pedestrian falls on your uncleared sidewalk
claims.law: NYC Administrative Code §7-210 (owner liable); the lease passes the cost to the tenant; CPLR §214 (three years to sue)
claims.trigger: A snowfall deadline passed with snow_ice_plan = none or the shortcut skip_snow_clearing on; at most one claim per winter
claims.note: Average claim $45,000: The Hartford 2025 review of small-business claims (slip, fall or customer injury; $20,000 in 2015). $2,500 (deductible and legal time) and the 25% premium increase are planning values: no public rate table was found. Under Cruz v Heights Broadway (First Department, 2023) the Administrative Code makes a tenant clear snow but does not make it liable in tort; the tenant pays through the indemnity clause of the lease, or directly if its own shoveling made the ice worse.

claims.name: Customer falls on your wet floor or doorstep
claims.law: New York common law of premises liability (negligence); NYC Administrative Code §7-210 for the sidewalk; 29 CFR 1910.22(a) for workers
claims.trigger: entrance_floor_safety = nothing through a month with 8 or more wet days; at most one claim per year
claims.note: Not a government penalty: the record models a lawsuit so the engine can price the risk. Max $45,000 is the average slip, fall or customer injury claim of a small business in The Hartford's 2025 review (Insurance Journal, December 10, 2025); it was $20,000 in 2015. Base $2,500 is my planning value for what an insured owner pays: a $1,000-$2,500 deductible plus a premium increase at renewal. The claim arrives months after the fall: the New York deadline to sue for personal injury is three years (CPLR §214).

claims.name: Pedestrian falls into your open cellar hatch
claims.law: NYC Administrative Code §7-210 (sidewalk hardware, including cellar doors); common-law negligence
claims.trigger: delivery_hatch_rule = open_and_go for six months in a place with a sidewalk hatch; at most one claim
claims.note: Courts treat cellar doors as part of the sidewalk an owner must keep safe; in a 2020-21 Appellate Division case the owner escaped liability because the doors were sound and it was the ground-floor tenant who had opened them unsafely, which points the claim at the shop. Cost fields reuse the fall-claim planning values.

monthlyClimate.station: New York Central Park, NOAA 1991-2020 normals (National Weather Service monthly almanacs)
monthlyClimate.note: Opened the twelve National Weather Service almanac PDFs for Central Park (nycjan.pdf to nycdec.pdf): 'Mean Max', 'Mean Avg', 'Mean Precip' and 'Mean Snow', all 1991-2020 normals. Precipitation sums to 49.52 inches and snow to 29.8. The highs differ by 0.1°F in six months from ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json, which averaged the daily normals. Days at 90°F or more are from the NWS table 'Average Number of 90°F+ Degree Days By Month' (averages over the whole record since 1869) and its yearly rows. Season snowfall is from the NWS monthly and seasonal snowfall table; its 2025-26 row was incomplete when opened (December 2025: 7.2 inches), so the 43.4-inch total for that winter stays a press figure. Other extremes: 100°F on July 2, 2026 and 2.07 inches of rain in one hour on July 14, 2025 (press and city releases, not opened).

drinkMixByTemperature.note: Opened United Baristas' analysis of one coffee shop (Ensemble, King's Cross, London, January-June): 'for every 1°C increase in the daily maximum temperature, cold coffees increased their share of sales by 2.2 percentage points'; 'Maximum daily temperature alone explains 92% of the variation'; in the coldest week (average high 4.9°C) 1.6% of coffees were cold, in the week of May 25 (29°C) more than 61%; their rule of thumb is 20% at 15°C, 30% at 20°C, 40% at 24°C, over 50% at 28°C. Verified: the slope (2.2 / 1.8 = 1.22 points per °F) and the anchor 20% at 59°F. Not verified: the +15 points I add for New York, which is my assumption from chain statements (Starbucks: about 75% of US beverage sales cold in summer 2022; Dunkin': more than half iced even in winter). The first pass anchored the curve at 20% at 40°F and overstated every month by about 8-10 points. measuredLondonCurveByMonth is the curve with no offset. Total orders move far less than the mix: Planalytics and the retail federation put the average weather swing in coffee sales at 5%.

comparisonsAbroad.finding: Heat above 25°C cut weekend restaurant bookings by about 18% (TheFork booking data); in the warm season German restaurants took 12% more orders but only 4% more revenue, and guests stayed for less time (Lightspeed, 1,600 restaurants, April 2024-March 2025).
comparisonsAbroad.lesson: Supports holding foot traffic flat and moving the mix in a New York heat wave: more, smaller, colder orders.

comparisonsAbroad.finding: A bank guide for cafe owners puts the fall in visits at 10-15% in sharp cold or abnormal heat and advises shifting to delivery and mobile points; Russian owners describe a 10-15% drop in a bad October and near-record days on warm weekends.
comparisonsAbroad.lesson: Same order of size as the New York rain and cold values (5-15%), from an unrelated market.

comparisonsAbroad.finding: When a customer falls on icy steps of a shop or cafe, the owner or the tenant of the premises answers; courts award moral damages (70,000 rubles in one Orenburg case) plus a consumer-law penalty of 50% of the award, and look for warning signs and video.
comparisonsAbroad.lesson: The duty at the door is not a New York peculiarity; what differs is the size of the claim ($45,000 average in the United States against about $1,000 there).

comparisonsAbroad.finding: Coffee shops in front of street works reported sales down 30% on the first day and 50% later (Seattle), a 36% fall over two years before closing (St. Louis), and a permanent closure after weeks of a dug-up sidewalk (Winnipeg).
comparisonsAbroad.lesson: The single New York figure (10-15% on West 10th Street) is at the mild end; a cafe whose own sidewalk is closed can lose half its trade.

nonObvious.text: A very small shop may legally share its carter.
nonObvious.why: A business that throws away less than 20 gallons of garbage a week may share private carter service with other businesses, under a written contract.

nonObvious.text: Flies are an autumn violation.
nonObvious.why: Citations for filth flies in restaurant inspections peaked in October 2025 (438) and were still at 351 in November, against 64 in February.

nonObvious.text: Rats are a summer problem on the street and a winter problem in the kitchen.
nonObvious.why: 311 rodent complaints peak in June (3,694 in 2025) and bottom in December (1,133); inspection citations for rats and mice inside restaurants peak in December and January.

nonObvious.text: The second dirty-sidewalk or sidewalk-sign ticket costs six times the first.
nonObvious.why: For commercial property the steps are $50, $300, $500, not the $50 and $100 quoted for homeowners.

nonObvious.text: An unanswered sanitation ticket multiplies itself.
nonObvious.why: OATH data since January 2025: a $100 snow summons became $350 in 41% of cases because nobody answered it; a $50 dirty-sidewalk summons became $450 and a $50 bin summons $300 in about a quarter of cases.

nonObvious.text: The snow deadline is counted from the minute the snow stops, and the shortest window (4 hours) falls exactly on your business hours.
nonObvious.why: A storm that ends at 10 AM must be cleared by 2 PM, in the lunch rush, by the same two people who run the bar.

nonObvious.text: The building owner is liable for a fall on the sidewalk, but the tenant usually pays.
nonObvious.why: Administrative Code §7-210 names the owner; the lease has an indemnity clause; courts hold the tenant itself liable only if its own shoveling made things worse.

nonObvious.text: Shoveling badly can be worse in court than not shoveling.
nonObvious.why: A tenant who piles snow that melts and refreezes across the walk has created the hazard, which is the one case where the tenant is liable in its own right.

nonObvious.text: Closing early for a storm still costs wages.
nonObvious.why: Call-in pay: three hours at the minimum wage for everyone who reported. Decide the evening before.

nonObvious.text: Ice melt sells out two days before the storm, every time.
nonObvious.why: January and February 2026: stores from Yonkers to the Hudson Valley were out; buy in November.

nonObvious.text: Heat does not empty a coffee shop; it changes what the shop sells.
nonObvious.why: Coffee brands gain a little traffic on very hot days while restaurants lose it; cold drinks gain 2.2 points of share per degree Celsius.

nonObvious.text: A missed coffee on a rainy day is never bought later.
nonObvious.why: The retail federation's weather report: daily coffee runs rebound within days, but the missed transactions are not made up.

nonObvious.text: The average sidewalk shed stays up for a year and a half, and you can know it is coming before you sign.
nonObvious.why: Facade inspections run on a public five-year cycle for every building over six stories; shed permits are open data.

nonObvious.text: You may hang a sign on the shed that hides your sign.
nonObvious.why: The Buildings Department bans advertising on sheds but allows a temporary sign directly in front of a storefront whose lawful sign is blocked.

nonObvious.text: The city pays nothing when its own construction empties your street.
nonObvious.why: Small Business Services' FAQ says there is no program or grant to reimburse lost revenue.

nonObvious.text: A street fair on your block can be a bad day.
nonObvious.why: The stalls stand between the crowd and your door and sell drinks; deliveries cannot reach you.

nonObvious.text: Being on the marathon course can cut you off from your own customers.
nonObvious.why: In 2026 the race changed its Bronx route for the first time in 15 years to restore access to local businesses.

nonObvious.text: A weekend subway shutdown costs a fifth of weekend sales, and it can last two years.
nonObvious.why: Greenpoint: the G train was out on about 40% of weekends from 2024; surveyed shops lost 20-24% on those weekends.

nonObvious.text: A bike lane that removes parking has not been shown to hurt sales.
nonObvious.why: On Ninth Avenue, local business sales rose up to 49% in three years against 3% for Manhattan (the city's own sales-tax study).

nonObvious.text: You must clean 18 inches of the street, not just the sidewalk, and it does not matter who dropped the litter.
nonObvious.why: DSNY rule for owners and tenants; agents come at fixed hours for each block.

nonObvious.text: A coffee cup with your logo in the corner basket is evidence against you.
nonObvious.why: The code presumes that the business named on garbage in a public litter basket put it there; in practice the charge is rare: 7 summonses since January 2025.

nonObvious.text: Ten flyers on lampposts are ten tickets.
nonObvious.why: Each poster is a separate $75 summons, $125 if ignored; 2,690 were written in 2026; a new shop was reportedly fined almost $9,000.

nonObvious.text: A sandwich board is legal only within 3 feet of your wall and up to 5 feet high.
nonObvious.why: Beyond that it is a sidewalk obstruction; under a shed or on a narrow sidewalk there may be no legal place for it.

nonObvious.text: Cooling the sidewalk through an open door is illegal for every store, but almost never ticketed.
nonObvious.why: About 40 summonses against single stores since January 2025, most at $250 (OATH data); DCWP reported 58 open-door violations in 2023.

nonObvious.text: Your insurance does not cover the two ways rain ruins a basement.
nonObvious.why: A business owner's policy excludes flood and sewer backup; the backup rider is cheap and separate.

nonObvious.text: The sewers are built for 1.75 inches of rain an hour, and that now happens several times a year.
nonObvious.why: Five storms exceeded it in 2023; July 14, 2025 brought 2.07 inches in an hour.

nonObvious.text: Con Edison pays for spoiled food only if its own equipment failed, for more than 12 hours, and you file within 30 days with a list.
nonObvious.why: Storm outages are excluded; the business cap is $12,900.

nonObvious.text: Snow brings power cuts a week later.
nonObvious.why: Road salt and meltwater corrode underground cables: 68% of the manhole events of 2014 came in January and February.

nonObvious.text: When the building next door is demolished, its rats move to you.
nonObvious.why: The law requires an exterminator before a demolition permit, which treats the site, not your basement.

nonObvious.text: After a blizzard nobody collects trash for days, in the same week the rats are hungriest.
nonObvious.why: February 2026: collection ran days behind while crews plowed.

nonObvious.text: A cafe that lives on office workers has a three-day week and a ten-month year.
nonObvious.why: Fridays are 12% of weekday office visits; August and December run a third below 2019.

nonObvious.text: The hour change in November costs afternoon sales for weeks.
nonObvious.why: Card spending falls 3.5% in the month after the clocks go back.

nonObvious.text: A world event in town is not a windfall for a shop that is not part of it.
nonObvious.why: After the 2026 World Cup only 29% of small businesses with a strong summer credited the tournament; those not showing matches more often lost sales to closures.

nonObvious.text: Nothing in New York law makes you pay extra on Christmas, and nothing stops your baristas from quitting if you do not.
nonObvious.why: Holiday premium pay is custom or contract, not statute.

nonObvious.text: Outdoor seats count toward the 20-seat bathroom rule and exist only on dry days between about 55 and 88 degrees.
nonObvious.why: The license fee is paid all year; the seats work perhaps half the days of the season.

nonObvious.text: A corner shop pays for its second window every time it snows.
nonObvious.why: Two frontages, the curb ramps and the hydrant are all yours to clear on the same clock.

nonObvious.text: The city can change the taste of your espresso.
nonObvious.why: In a drought or during aqueduct repairs the reservoir blend changes; in November 2024 the city paused an aqueduct repair to bring more water in. The effect on hardness and taste is from owner lore and was not confirmed in this session.

kitAdditions.note: The validator requires every required setup item to be in all three kits, so these two are sent with required: false. Bins with lids are required by law for every business that sets trash at the curb; the snow kit is needed unless the contractor option of snow_ice_plan is chosen. Suggested: add both to lean, standard and premium with qty 1 and then set required: true.

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Sanitation enforcement agents walk commercial blocks in two fixed one-hour periods a day that depend on the address, and after every snowfall. They write a summons on the spot; no warning is required. The summons is answered at the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings or paid; an unanswered one defaults to the maximum penalty.
officials.note: Opened NYC311: 'Commercial property enforcement times are limited to two 1-hour periods per day. The exact times depend on the Sanitation section the address is located in.' Default penalties are from the OATH hearings data ($350 for snow, $450 for a commercial dirty sidewalk, $300 for a bin violation). In 2026 to mid-November Sanitation agents wrote more than 450,000 summonses of all kinds.

levers.name: Snow and ice at your door

options.label: Staff shovel and salt on the clock, within the legal window
Seasonal contract: a crew clears and salts after every snowfall
Leave it: the sun will melt it

levers.note: Charged only in December-March (activeMonths is a new field). Staff option: Central Park averages about 11 days a season with measurable snow (1991-2020 normals in ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json: Dec 2.1, Jan 3.7, Feb 3.2, Mar 2.0), about 2.75 a month; one hour of a $17.00 worker each time plus a second pass for refreeze = 2.75 x 1.5 h x $17 = $70, plus about $20 of ice melt. Contractor: no New York storefront price was found; vendor guides quote $350-$1,500 per visit for commercial lots in Brooklyn and $2,000-$10,000 a season nationally, which is plowing, not a 20-foot sidewalk. $400 a month ($1,600 a season) is my planning value for a shovel-only sidewalk contract: get three local quotes. The summons is $100 per snowfall and $350 if ignored (OATH data). The -3% demand of 'none' applies only on days with snow or ice on the ground (see extra.mechanics.sidewalk_clock).

levers.name: Wet floor at the entrance

options.label: Rented entrance mats swapped weekly, wet-floor signs, mop every hour in bad weather
A towel by the door

levers.note: No price list for mat rental in New York was found; $80 a month (two mats, weekly swap) is my planning value from uniform-service quotes I could not open. The reason the lever exists is the insurer's number: The Hartford's 2025 ten-year review puts the average slip, fall or customer injury claim of a small business at $45,000, up from $20,000 in 2015, and one in five small-business liability claims is now a fall.

levers.name: When a storm is forecast

options.label: Open as usual with the full schedule
Open with whoever lives close; cancel the other shifts the night before
Close on warning days and tell staff the evening before

levers.note: Applies only on days with a National Weather Service warning (blizzard, winter storm, flash flood, tropical storm). open_as_usual: full wages against 40% of normal traffic, and workers who cannot get in are simply absent. skeleton_crew: wages for half the staff; shifts cancelled the night before cost nothing. close_for_the_day: no sales and no wages if staff were told before they reported; anyone who already reported is owed call-in pay of 3 hours at the minimum wage (12 NYCRR §146-1.5; the State Labor Department applies it to weather closings). The effects written here are month-level placeholders: 1-2 warning days a month in winter. The shortcut storm_day_no_call_in_pay is the illegal variant.

levers.name: Trash: bins and pickups

options.label: Lidded bins, private carter three nights a week
Lidded bins, carter six nights a week

levers.note: The pack already charges $250 a month for the carter (monthlyCosts.waste); the costs here are differences from it. Six pickups instead of three: no published New York price was found (each waste zone has its own maximum-rate table); +$180 is my planning value, about 70% more for twice the stops. Three pickups a week means food waste sits two nights: in June-September that feeds the rodent score (extra.mechanics.trash_and_rodent_pressure). Putting bags on the curb without bins is the shortcut bags_on_curb.

levers.name: Your stretch of sidewalk

options.label: Sweep at opening and before closing, out to 18 inches into the street
Sweep twice a day and power-wash once a month
It is the city's sidewalk

levers.note: Sweeping: 10 minutes a day of a $17.00 worker x 30 days = $85. Power wash: $150 a visit is my planning value for a 20-foot storefront; no New York price list was found. The duty is real: DSNY makes owners and tenants clean the sidewalk and the gutter 18 inches into the street, even when someone else dropped the litter.

levers.name: Summer: air conditioning and the door

options.label: Air conditioner serviced in spring, door kept shut
Run it until it breaks

levers.note: Charged May-September. $60 a month = one spring service visit of about $300 spread over five months (planning value). 'unserviced' has no fine; it decides whether the heat_wave_ac_failure event hits this shop (rule 4: the breakdown follows from the choice, not from dice). Propping the door open with the air conditioning on is the shortcut ac_with_open_door.

levers.name: A sidewalk shed over your door

options.label: Wait for it to come down
Hang a temporary sign on the shed and light your entrance
Lawyer letter for a rent credit; report idle months to 311

levers.note: Only shown while a shed covers the storefront. Sign: the Buildings Department lets a business whose lawful sign is blocked put a temporary sign on the face of the shed directly in front of the storefront; $150 a month = a $1,200 banner and LED strip written off over 8 months (planning value). The +3% recovers about half of the measured loss (3.5-9.7% of weekly transactions). Rent credit: nothing in the law gives a tenant a credit for a shed; it is whatever the lease says. -5% of rent for a $250-a-month lawyer retainer is my estimate of a negotiated outcome, not a right. Local Law 48 of 2025 fines the building owner for months with no work, which is the tenant's leverage.

levers.name: When the street is torn up or the train is out

options.label: Change nothing
'We are open' signs at both corners, a punch card for regulars
Push pickup orders and delivery while the block is hard to reach

levers.note: Only shown during a street, subway or utility disruption. The city pays nothing for lost sales (Small Business Services FAQ, 2022), so the owner pays for any mitigation. $200 = printed signs and a 10th-drink-free card at about 1% of sales; +3% is my estimate of what it wins back out of a 10-22% loss. Delivery: $100 of listing promotion; delivery orders also pay the platform commission that the pack models elsewhere.

levers.name: Parade, fair or race on your street

options.label: A normal day
Extra barista, double pastry order, cups stocked the night before
Sell five fast items from the door, no seating

levers.note: Applies on announced event days only. $120 = one extra 7-hour shift at $17.00. Deliveries cannot reach a closed street, so stock arrives the day before. The capacity gains are month-level placeholders; on the day itself the window menu roughly doubles orders per hour (design value). The crowd is only worth what you can serve.

levers.name: Seats outside

options.label: No outdoor seats
Licensed sidewalk cafe: 4 tables against your wall
Licensed roadway cafe in the parking lane, now allowed all year

levers.note: Sidewalk: license $1,050 for four years ($22 a month) plus the yearly consent fee, $6 a square foot in about 80% of the city (up to $31 in Manhattan below 125th Street): 100 sq ft x $6 / 12 = $50; furniture $1,100 written off over four years = $23. Total $95 at the $6 rate; at $31 the fee alone is $258 a month. Roadway: license $22 a month; consent fee $5-$25 a square foot (160 sq ft x $8 / 12 = $107); a code-compliant platform and barriers of about $7,000 over two years = $290. The roadway numbers other than the fee range are my planning values. Seats count only on dry days between about 55°F and 88°F (extra.mechanics.outdoor_seat_days). The existing rule card says approval took most applicants over 19 months, and outdoor seats count toward the 20-seat bathroom line. Since August 31, 2026 roadway cafes may stay up all year under a separate license; the winter rules are still being written.

levers.name: Basement and heavy rain

options.label: Stock on the basement floor, standard insurance
Stock on racks 6 inches up, water-backup rider on the policy, door dam for flood warnings
Backwater valve on the sewer line, sump pump, flood policy

levers.note: basic: water-backup endorsement $50-$250 a year on consumer policies ($15 a month at the middle; no commercial quote was found) + four dunnage racks and a door barrier, about $480 over two years = $20. full: backwater valve installed for about $3,000 and a sump pump for $1,500, written off over five years = $75, plus a commercial flood policy at a planning value of $1,400 a year = $115. A standard business owner's policy covers neither flood nor sewer backup. The lever decides how much the flash_flood_warning and sewer_backup events cost: none = full loss, basic = stock saved and cleanup insured, full = no water.

levers.name: Menu through the year

options.label: One menu all year
Cold-brew and iced specials in summer, spiced and hot specials from September

levers.note: $150 = menu printing, syrups and a second cold-brew keg (planning value). +3% demand is my estimate: Toast's 2025 data shows cold brew orders peaking in July at 35% above the yearly average and regular coffee peaking in December and March; Placer.ai measured Starbucks' pumpkin-menu launch day on August 25, 2026 at 25.7% above its daily average for the year. A small shop gets a fraction of that, and only if the special exists.

levers.name: Smoke days

options.label: Nothing special
High-grade filter in the air handler, a portable air cleaner, masks for staff

levers.note: $40 = a MERV-13 filter changed quarterly, a $300 HEPA unit over three years and a box of KN95 masks (planning value). On a smoke day the option keeps the room usable: the shop loses street traffic but not the customers already inside, and staff are not sent home. Effects are applied by the wildfire_smoke_day event.

levers.name: Keeping rodents out

options.label: Rely on the exterminator
Door sweeps, sealed pipe gaps, rodent-proof bins, trash out of the shop every night

levers.note: $60 = $700 of door sweeps, steel wool, sealant and two steel bins over two years, plus ten minutes of closing labor a day. Works with the existing pest_control lever: an exterminator treats, sealing keeps them out. It decides whether the seasonal pressure events (construction next door, summer peak, first cold week) turn into the existing pest_activity violation.

levers.name: Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's Day

options.label: Closed on the three big holidays
Open 8 to 2 with volunteers at time-and-a-half
Open all day at regular pay

levers.note: New York has no rule that makes a private employer pay a premium for work on a holiday; holiday pay exists only where a contract or the shop's own policy promises it (law-firm guide; the State Labor Department text was not opened). Time-and-a-half is a custom, and the price of keeping a crew: $110 = two baristas x 6 hours x $8.50 premium, once in the month. A holiday morning on a residential block is one of the busiest of the year because everything else is closed; in an office district it is dead. +1% of the month is my estimate for one strong day. Regular pay on Christmas costs goodwill: the quality effect is a design value that should feed turnover in D05.

levers.name: Cold-proofing the shop

options.label: Turn the heat down at night and hope
Insulated pipes, heat held at 55°F overnight, door closer and draft strip
All of that plus a temporary winter vestibule at the door, November 15 to April 15

levers.note: pipes_and_door: $150 of pipe insulation and weather-stripping and a $120 door closer over five cold months, plus about $40 a month of extra heat = $70 (planning values). vestibule: a sign maker's guide says a temporary storm enclosure may stand from November 15 to April 15, may project 18 inches for most businesses and up to 25 square feet for restaurants if 5 feet of sidewalk stay clear (Building Code §3202.3.2.1), and needs no Buildings Department permit inside those limits; the official text was not opened. $450 a month = a made-to-measure vinyl and aluminum vestibule with installation, removal and storage at about $2,250 a season (my planning value; get quotes), plus the $70. It keeps the tables by the door usable (door_draft_tables) and gives the queue a place out of the wind. 'none' decides whether frozen_pipe hits the shop: water and freezing damage is 20% of small-business claims and averages $34,600 (The Hartford, 2025).

levers.name: If the power goes out

options.label: Nothing prepared
Fridge thermometers and a log, ice chests, battery lights, card reader that works offline, claim form ready

levers.note: $15 a month = about $350 of coolers, thermometers and lanterns over two years (planning value). With basic, an outage of up to 8 hours loses no stock and the shop can sell batch coffee and pastries for cash or offline card; with none, milk above 41°F for more than two hours is discarded (the existing spoiled_food rule) and the Con Edison claim fails for lack of an itemized list. D03 owns generators and equipment protection.

levers.name: Sidewalk cellar doors during deliveries

options.label: Cones out and one person stays at the open hatch
Open the doors and carry on

levers.note: Only for places with a sidewalk hatch. $45 = 10 minutes of a second worker on 16 delivery days. Practitioner summaries of the Administrative Code: when cellar doors are open someone must stay there to steer people around the opening; doors must sit flush and bear weight. A fall is a claim under §7-210, the same route as the icy sidewalk.

levers.name: After closing

options.label: Lock the door, leave the float in the till
Monitored alarm, camera, cash out of the till every night

levers.note: $55 = alarm monitoring at about $40 and a camera subscription at $15 (planning values; a roll-down gate, where the landlord allows one, is a setup cost for D03). Burglary and theft are 20% of small-business claims in The Hartford's 2025 review. The option decides the break_in event.

shortcuts.name: Do not clear the snow
shortcuts.what: Nobody shovels or salts your sidewalk after a snowfall. You save the labor. A sanitation agent can ticket you the same day, and if someone falls on your ice the claim follows you for three years.

shortcuts.name: Send staff home in a storm with no pay
shortcuts.what: You close an hour into the storm and pay only the minutes worked. The law says everyone who reported is owed at least three hours.

shortcuts.name: Trash bags on the curb, no bins
shortcuts.what: You skip the lidded bins and put black bags straight on the sidewalk. Since March 2024 every business must use bins with secure lids. Bags also feed the rats on your own block.

shortcuts.name: Use the corner litter basket instead of a carter
shortcuts.what: Staff carry the shop's trash to the city basket on the corner. You save the private carter's bill. City baskets are for pedestrians only, and a cup with your logo in the bag is all the proof an agent needs.

shortcuts.name: Everything in one bag
shortcuts.what: No sorting: cardboard, milk jugs and trash go out together and the carter charges less. Businesses must separate recyclables.

shortcuts.name: Tape flyers to lampposts
shortcuts.what: Fifty flyers on poles and construction fences instead of paid ads. Posting on public property is illegal, and each flyer is its own ticket.

shortcuts.name: A-frame sign and bench out in the walkway
shortcuts.what: You put the sandwich board and a bench where people have to walk around them. More passers-by notice the shop. Anything more than 3 feet from your wall is an obstruction.

shortcuts.name: Door propped open with the air conditioning on
shortcuts.what: An open door and a wave of cold air pull people in off a hot sidewalk. It is illegal for every store in the city, and it adds to your electric bill.

shortcuts.name: Speaker in the doorway
shortcuts.what: Music played out onto the sidewalk pulls people in. Using sound to advertise in front of a business is banned, and the neighbors upstairs have 311 on speed dial.

violations.name: Snow or ice left on the sidewalk past the legal deadline
violations.criminal: None. The larger exposure is civil: a pedestrian who falls on the uncleared sidewalk can sue the building owner (Administrative Code §7-210), and most store leases make the tenant pay the owner back.
violations.note: Opened NYC311 'Snow or Ice on Sidewalk': if the snow stops between 7 AM and 5 PM, clear within 4 hours; 5 PM to 9 PM, within 14 hours; 9 PM to 7 AM, by 11 AM. Clear a path at least 4 feet wide; on a corner, clear access to the crosswalk and the pedestrian ramp; shovel bus stops without shelters and fire hydrants; spread salt or sand if the ground is frozen; do not shovel snow into a street, crosswalk or bike lane. The article names the owner of the building or lot and says 'a fine (up to $250)'. Penalties actually imposed, counted from the OATH hearings data set (charge AS21, 'Snow, ice, dirt on sidewalks', violations since January 1, 2025): $100 in 18,026 cases, $350 in 14,548 cases that defaulted, $130 in 1,657, dismissed in 1,403. So the ticket is $100 and becomes $350 if the summons is ignored. Volume: 9,456 summonses for January-March 2026 (January 5,852; February 3,481; March 123) and 54,089 'Snow or Ice' complaints to 311 between January 20 and March 15, 2026. Each uncleared snowfall is a new summons.

violations.name: Call-in pay not paid after a weather closing
violations.law: 12 NYCRR §146-1.5 (Hospitality Industry Wage Order); NY Labor Law §198(1-a)
violations.criminal: None for a first case; repeated willful non-payment of wages is a misdemeanor under Labor Law §198-a.
violations.note: Opened the Attorney General's wage page: 'If you are required or permitted to report to work, even if you are not assigned actual work, you may be entitled to call-in pay. In most cases, restaurant or hotel workers should receive three hours' pay at the appropriate minimum wage.' That the State Labor Department applies it to weather closings is from law-firm advisories (not opened). Saved amount: one sent-home shift per worker per winter month, 3 h x $17.00 = $51, less about an hour actually paid = $35. Unpaid wages are owed back with 100% liquidated damages (Labor Law §198(1-a)), hence pctOfSaved 2, as for the other wage violations in the pack.

violations.name: Dirty sidewalk or gutter in front of the shop
violations.note: Counted from the OATH hearings data set, violations since January 1, 2025, charges for commercial, manufacturing, industrial and mixed-use property under §16-118: 'Dirty sidewalk' first offense $50 (3,522 cases; $450 in 1,182 defaulted cases), second $300, third $500; 'Fail to clean 18 inches into street' the same steps ($50 in 4,431 cases, $450 in 1,397 defaults; second $300, third $500). In 2026 to mid-November: 2,977 first-offense commercial dirty-sidewalk summonses and 3,468 for the 18 inches. Opened NYC311: owners must clean the sidewalk, tree beds and gutter and 'the area extending 18 inches into the street from the curb', 'even if someone else caused the dirty condition'; commercial enforcement is 'limited to two 1-hour periods per day' that depend on the address; 'when businesses are closed they must arrange to have the area maintained'. The earlier figure ($100 after the first) was wrong for commercial property.

violations.name: Trash set out in bags or at the wrong time
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-120; DSNY set-out and containerization rules for businesses
violations.note: Opened NYC311 'Waste Disposal for Businesses': 'As of March 1, 2024, all businesses in NYC must use bins with secure lids when setting out trash for collection'; bins may go to the curb 1 hour before closing or after 8 PM; recycling in bags or bundles after 8 PM; all bins off the curb by the time the business reopens; stored inside or within 3 feet of the building line; it is illegal to chain bins to public property; fines $50 for a first offense, $100 for a second, $200 for all later ones. The city does not sell bins to businesses. OATH data, violations since January 1, 2025: 'Improper receptacle, non-residential, 1st' $50 in 10,763 cases and $300 in 5,452 defaults; second offense $100, third $200; 'placed out prior to one hour of closing' $50 (1,064) or $300 on default (404); 'failure to remove receptacles' $50 (994) or $300 (324). In 2026 to mid-November: 4,842, 726 and 546 summonses.

violations.name: Business trash in a public litter basket
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-120(e); §16-116 (businesses must use a licensed private carter)
violations.note: DSNY collection and set-out laws for businesses, as quoted by web search: 'Under no circumstances can a merchant dispose of any garbage or recyclable materials in a DSNY litter basket'; $100 first offense, $250 second, $350 third and later. The code presumes that the person whose name appears on garbage found in the basket put it there. Second pass: the OATH hearings data set shows this charge ('Improper disposal, DSNY litter basket, 1st offense') only 7 times since January 1, 2025, with $50 or $130 imposed or the case dismissed, so it is rarely ticketed and the $100-$250-$350 schedule quoted from the DSNY page was not confirmed. Opened NYC311: a business must hire a private carter or register as a self-hauler with the Business Integrity Commission, and must post the carter's decal; businesses that throw away less than 20 gallons a week may share a carter.

violations.name: Recyclables not separated
violations.note: DSNY business pages as quoted by web search: $100 first offense, $200 second, $400 third and later for failing to separate recyclables. The section numbers are from memory and need a check against the code.

violations.name: Flyers posted on public property
violations.note: Counted from the OATH hearings data set (charge AS30, 'Illegal posting of handbill notice', §10-119), violations since January 1, 2025: $75 where the respondent paid or was found in violation (584 cases), $125 in 5,349 defaulted cases and $105 in 741; 2,690 summonses in 2026 to mid-November. Each posting is its own summons. Base $750 = ten flyers at $75. Max $9,000 is a press report of one Clinton Hill shop fined almost that much (DNAinfo), not verified. Opened NYC311: the Sanitation Department removes postings from public property and, if it can identify who is responsible, 'may give them a violation'.

violations.name: Sign, bench or goods blocking the sidewalk
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118 (sidewalk obstruction); NYC311: signs within 3 feet of the building and no higher than 5 feet
violations.note: Counted from the OATH hearings data set, violations since January 1, 2025: 'Sidewalk obstruction, commercial/manufacturing/industrial/mixed use' first offense $50 (7,526 cases; $450 in 2,720 defaults), second $300, third $500; 5,455 first-offense summonses in 2026 to mid-November. Opened NYC311 'Sidewalk Obstruction': 'Sandwich and A-frame signs must not extend more than 3 feet into the sidewalk from the building' and must not 'be higher than 5 feet'. The $100-$300 range from 2015 press reports was wrong.

violations.name: Air conditioning running with the door open
violations.note: Counted from the OATH hearings data set, violations since January 1, 2025, charge 'Business kept exterior door or window open while an air conditioner... was operating' under §20-910(b): about 40 cases against single stores, with $250 imposed most often (16 cases), $400-$550 in a few and 8 dismissed; 9 cases against chain stores at $500 to $1,500. So it is real but rare: roughly two tickets a month citywide. The delivery exception and the rule's reach to stores of every size are from the DCWP flyer as quoted by web search (nyc.gov could not be opened).

violations.name: Music from the shop audible outside or in the apartments above
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §24-244(b) (sound devices used to attract attention to a business) and §24-231 (commercial music: 42 dB(A) inside a nearby residence)
violations.note: Counted from the OATH hearings data set, violations since January 1, 2025, charge 'Made, caused or permitted music from a commercial establishment over permitted levels': first offense $2,000 in 16 cases, $8,000 in 27 defaulted cases, $0 in 4 (the cure the DEP notice describes); second offense $4,000 or $16,000 on default; third $24,000 on default. A separate charge, 'Unreasonable noise from a sound reproduction device', runs $440, or $1,750 on default. The 42 dB(A) limit inside a neighbor's home and the ban on speakers used to draw customers (§24-244(b)) are from DEP material and a court decision as quoted by web search.

ruleCards.title: The snow clock
ruleCards.text: When snow stops between 7 AM and 5 PM you have 4 hours to clear your sidewalk; 5 PM to 9 PM, 14 hours; overnight, until 11 AM. A 4-foot path, nothing shoveled into the street. The ticket is $100 per snowfall, and $350 if you ignore the summons.

ruleCards.title: Who pays when someone falls
ruleCards.text: In New York City the building owner, not the city, is liable when someone is hurt on the sidewalk in front (Administrative Code §7-210). Read your lease: most make the store clear the snow and pay the owner back. The average fall claim is $45,000.

ruleCards.title: Sending staff home in a storm
ruleCards.text: Close early for weather and you still owe pay: a restaurant worker who reports for a shift and is sent home is owed three hours at the minimum wage in most cases. Decide before they travel, not after.

ruleCards.title: Bins with lids
ruleCards.text: Since March 1, 2024 every NYC business must set out trash in bins with secure lids: out one hour before closing or after 8 PM, back in before you reopen. Bags on the curb cost $50, then $100, then $200. Ignore the summons and it is $300.

ruleCards.title: 18 inches into the street
ruleCards.text: You must keep your sidewalk clean and the gutter too, 18 inches out from the curb, even if someone else dropped the litter. For a business: $50 the first time, $300 the second, $500 the third. Agents come in two fixed hours a day.

ruleCards.title: The corner basket is not yours
ruleCards.text: City litter baskets are for pedestrians. Shop trash in one is illegal, and a cup with your name on it counts as proof. Every business must hire a licensed private carter or register to haul its own; under 20 gallons a week, you may share a carter.

ruleCards.title: Shut the door
ruleCards.text: No store in New York City may run air conditioning with its doors or windows open (Local Law 92 of 2015). The only exception is a door open for deliveries. A first ticket is $250; chain stores pay $500 and up.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk sheds
ruleCards.text: A shed over your door cuts restaurant and bar transactions by 3.5-9.7% a week. Since 2025 shed permits last 90 days, not a year, and owners pay monthly penalties when no work is done. You may hang a temporary sign on the shed in front of your store.

ruleCards.title: Nobody pays for the dig
ruleCards.text: When the city tears up your street, your sales are your problem. The City's own FAQ: it 'does not have any programs or grants to reimburse a business for lost revenue because of construction.' Ask about the project before you sign a lease.

ruleCards.title: A-frame signs
ruleCards.text: A sandwich board may stand no more than 3 feet out from your wall and no higher than 5 feet. Further out it is a sidewalk obstruction: $50 the first time, $300 the second, $500 the third, and $450 if you ignore the first summons.

ruleCards.title: Flyers on poles
ruleCards.text: Taping flyers to lampposts, mailboxes or fences is illegal posting: $75 for each flyer, $125 if you ignore the summons. Ten flyers is ten tickets. One new Brooklyn shop was reportedly fined almost $9,000.

ruleCards.title: Congestion Relief Zone
ruleCards.text: Below 60th Street in Manhattan cars pay $9 a day at peak hours; delivery trucks pay $14.40 or $21.60 every time they enter. In year one foot traffic in the zone rose 3.4% against 1.4% for the borough, and truck speeds rose 5.6%.

ruleCards.title: Rain is not in the policy
ruleCards.text: A standard business owner's policy pays for neither flood nor sewer backup. City sewers are built for at most 1.75 inches of rain an hour; on September 29, 2023 parts of Brooklyn got over 3. A water-backup rider costs roughly $50-$250 a year.

ruleCards.title: When the power goes out
ruleCards.text: If a failure in Con Edison's local grid leaves you dark for more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, a business can claim spoiled perishables, up to $12,900, within 30 days. Storm outages are not paid.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor dining, all year
ruleCards.text: Sidewalk cafes may operate all year, and since 2026 roadway cafes may too, under a year-round license with higher fees. The license is $1,050 for four years, or $2,100 for sidewalk and roadway together, plus a yearly fee set by location and size.

ruleCards.title: Smoke days
ruleCards.text: An Air Quality Index above 150 is unhealthy for everyone. In July 2026 Canadian wildfire smoke pushed New York City to 289, second only to June 2023. No law makes you close, but outdoor seats are useless and staff should not work outside.

ruleCards.title: Holiday pay
ruleCards.text: New York law does not require a private employer to pay extra for work on Thanksgiving or Christmas. Time-and-a-half is a custom, not a rule, unless your own handbook promises it. Overtime after 40 hours and the spread-of-hours hour still apply.

ruleCards.title: The office week
ruleCards.text: Offices fill on Tuesday to Thursday. From January to October 2025 only 12.4% of weekday office visits fell on a Friday, and August and December run about a third below 2019. A cafe that lives on office workers has a three-day week.

ruleCards.title: A corner means two sidewalks
ruleCards.text: On a corner you clear both frontages plus access to the crosswalk and the curb ramp, and you must shovel out the fire hydrant and any bus stop without a shelter. Same clock: 4 hours after daytime snow. A corner shop shovels twice as much.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk cellar doors
ruleCards.text: While your sidewalk hatch is open, someone must stand by it and steer people around the hole. Closed, the doors must sit flush and hold weight. A fall into an open hatch is a lawsuit against the building, and your lease sends the bill to you.

ruleCards.title: Music and the neighbors
ruleCards.text: You may not use a speaker to draw customers on the sidewalk. Music from a business may not exceed 42 dB(A) inside a neighbor's apartment. A first violation is $2,000, cut to $0 if you fix it and certify the fix, and $8,000 if you ignore it.

ruleCards.title: Fines are under review
ruleCards.text: Executive Order 11 (January 14, 2026) told city agencies to review rules and fines on small businesses and propose cuts, warnings and cure periods. An earlier round changed 116 rules, most of them rarely used. Until a fine is changed, it stands.

ruleCards.title: The most common claim
ruleCards.text: Water and freezing damage is one of the three most common small-business insurance claims, 20% of the total, and averages $34,600. A burst pipe on one cold night can cost more than a year of profit.

ruleCards.title: Winter vestibule
ruleCards.text: A temporary storm enclosure may stand at your door from November 15 to April 15. For most stores it may stick out 18 inches; for an eating place up to 25 square feet, with 5 feet of sidewalk left clear. Inside those limits no building permit is needed.

ruleCards.title: A broken sidewalk is the owner's to fix
ruleCards.text: When the city marks a sidewalk defect, the property owner has 75 days to repair it. There is no fine, but after 75 days the city may do the work and bill the owner. Most store leases pass sidewalk repairs to the tenant.

reports.name: Report a dirty sidewalk, trash bags or uncleared snow (311)
reports.text: The Sanitation Department sends an enforcement agent to the address. If the sidewalk is clean and the bins are out properly, you get a warning for a false report.

reports.name: Report a store cooling the street (311)
reports.text: Consumer and Worker Protection checks whether the door is propped open with the air conditioning on.

events.name: Sidewalk shed goes up on your block
events.text: Scaffolding covers your storefront while the building repairs its facade. Fewer people notice the shop, and nobody can tell you when it comes down.
events.note: Fix of the existing event (was 0.9 for 3 months, both my predecessor's estimates). The city's 2024 study with Mastercard: restaurants and bars under a shed saw weekly transactions fall 3.5-9.7% in the six months after it went up; Manhattan businesses lost $3,900-$9,500 a month. 0.93 is the midpoint (6.6%). Length: the average shed permit in March 2026 was 557 days old (West Side Rag analysis of Buildings Department data), so 12 months is still short; the engine caps an event at a season.

events.name: January slump
events.text: The slowest month of the coffee year: bills, resolutions and cold.
events.note: Short form of extra.eventCatalog.january_slump for the current engine. Starbucks: January is its lowest month. -8% is my estimate for an independent.

events.name: Wildfire smoke
events.text: Smoke from Canadian wildfires pushes the Air Quality Index over 150 for three days. People stay inside.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event: three days at 0.8 = 2% of a month. Index 289 on July 16-19, 2026; 465-484 in June 2023.

events.name: No weekend trains at your station
events.text: Signal work shuts your subway line on weekends. Shops near the stations lose a fifth of their weekend sales.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event. Greenpoint survey 2025-26: sales down 20-24% on shutdown weekends.

events.name: Water main replacement on your block
events.text: The street is fenced and trenched for a year. The city pays nothing for the sales you lose.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event. One West 10th Street shop: receipts down 10-15%.

events.name: The clocks go back
events.text: Dark at five. Afternoon walk-ins thin out for two months.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event. JPMorgan Chase Institute: daily card spending -3.5% after the clocks go back.

events.name: Con Edison rates rise
events.text: A three-year Con Edison rate plan took effect on January 1, 2026: a typical commercial electric bill is up about 3% this year, with further steps in 2027 and 2028.
events.note: Opened the Department of Public Service summary of the electric rate case: the Commission granted increases in annual electric revenue of $234 million, $409.7 million and $421.1 million over three rate years, 'a 2.8%, 2.8%, and 2.8% increase in total revenues'. Its bill table: a commercial customer using 10,800 kWh a month pays $83.25 more a month in year one (+3.1% of the total bill), then +$61.57 (+2.2%) and +$64.24 (+2.3%); a 425 kWh household +$5.27 (+3.6%). The first pass used 3.5% from the press; 1.031 is the commercial row. Replaces the deck's +5% card for January-February.

events.name: Blizzard
events.text: A foot of snow. The city asks people to stay home for two days, and you have four hours to clear your sidewalk when it stops.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event: two days at 0.4 = 4% of a month, rounded.

setup.name: Two rigid trash bins with secure lids
setup.note: Required since March 1, 2024 for every business that sets trash at the curb (opened NYC311: 'all businesses in NYC must use bins with secure lids'; 'The City does not sell or give away trash or recycling bins to commercial businesses'). Price is my planning value: two 44-gallon rigid bins with locking lids at about $90 each from a restaurant supplier. They live inside or within 3 feet of the building line and take about 8 square feet of floor.

setup.name: Snow shovel, ice scraper, salt spreader, four bags of ice melt
setup.note: Planning value: shovel $35, scraper $20, hand spreader $25, four 50 lb bags at about $20. Buy in November: stores ran out before the January and February 2026 storms. Not needed with the contractor option of snow_ice_plan.

setup.name: Two commercial entrance mats and wet-floor signs
setup.note: Alternative to the rented mats in the lever entrance_floor_safety: two 4 x 6 foot scraper mats at about $110 each and two signs at $20. Planning values.

setup.name: Dunnage racks: keep stock 6 inches off the basement floor
setup.note: Four racks at about $80 (planning value). Part of flood_protection = basic. The Health Code also requires food to be stored off the floor; the exact height and code number belong to D08.
